first.title: The first five minutes
first.body: Your feelings are real and they are not the focus right now. The instinct is to explain what you meant, or to fall apart — both land on the other person as being told it did not happen, or as a job to manage you.
scripts: “Can you help me understand what just happened? I don't want this to happen again.”
first.note: Then stop talking and listen to the answer, including if the answer is that they want you to go away.

descriptions.note: HAND-WRITTEN plain-language descriptions, for a reader who has never encountered a substance and does not know what it is. PsychonautWiki cannot supply these: its `summary` field is a scraped warning box that is frequently junk ("Summary sheet: MDMA MDMA"), and its `effects` field returns only the substance's own name. Both were checked against the live API on 2026-08-10 before writing these by hand. A second batch was written on 2026-08-15 for substances whose ordinary identity IS the description - a supplement, a spice, an over-the-counter box, a prescription somebody already holds. Those did not need a published effects write-up to be describable, and leaving them blank was the wrong call: a reader who does not know that myristicin is nutmeg cannot assess anything else on the page. Where the effects genuinely are not documented, the description says so rather than inventing them.
rules: Say what it IS and what people take it FOR. Someone who does not know cannot assess a warning about it.
No dosing, no route advice, no how-to. Dose ranges already live in their own section with their own caveats.
Neither advertise nor frighten. 'Euphoric' oversells; 'deadly poison' is the fear-based framing EVIDENCE.md rejects. Describe.
Name the ordinary medical use where there is one - most people meet oxycodone, ketamine and diazepam in a hospital first.
Plain words. Roughly an 8th-grade reading level, no pharmacology unless it changes what someone would do.
Where the thing has an ordinary identity - a supplement, a spice, an OTC box, a prescription - lead with that. What it says on the packaging is a checkable fact and it is what the reader recognizes.
Where nobody has published what it DOES, say so plainly and still say what it IS. An absence of effects data is not an absence of identity.

descriptions.alcohol: The drug in beer, wine and spirits. Chemically it is ethanol. It is a depressant, so it slows the brain and body. That is what makes people relaxed, talkative and unsteady. Coordination, judgement and memory get worse as the dose goes up. The liver clears it at a roughly fixed rate per hour.
descriptions.cannabis: The dried flower of the cannabis plant, smoked, vaped or eaten. Effects vary a lot between people and between strains. Usually it brings relaxation, changed senses and hunger. Some people get anxiety or a racing heart instead. Eaten, it comes on slowly and lasts far longer.
descriptions.mdma: A stimulant that also does something to your feelings, sold as ecstasy or molly, in pills or powder. People take it for warmth, closeness and energy, mostly around other people and music. It pushes up your body temperature and heart rate. A lot of what gets sold under these names is not MDMA at all.
descriptions.lsd: A psychedelic, usually sold on small squares of blotter paper. It changes how you see, think and feel for eight to twelve hours, which is longer than most people expect the first time. Chemically it is a semi-synthetic ergoline, active in the microgram range: a dose is a few tens of millionths of a gram.
descriptions.psilocybin-mushrooms: Mushrooms containing psilocybin, sometimes called magic mushrooms or shrooms, usually eaten dried or brewed into tea. They bring visual changes, shifts in thinking and mood, and often strong emotion, for about four to six hours. The body converts psilocybin into psilocin, which is the compound that does the work.
descriptions.ketamine: An anesthetic used in hospitals and by vets, also used as a powder recreationally. It makes you feel detached from your body and your surroundings. At higher amounts, movement and response stop altogether. That is called a k-hole. It is a dissociative, acting mainly by blocking NMDA receptors.
descriptions.cocaine: A stimulant made from the coca plant, sold as a white powder. It makes you alert, confident and full of energy, often for under an hour. That short run is why people keep going back for more. It strains the heart. Mixed with alcohol, the body makes a third substance that is harder on the heart than either alone.
descriptions.crack-cocaine: Cocaine cooked into a smokable rock. Same drug as powder cocaine. Smoking gets it there faster and it wears off sooner. So people redose more often, and dependence builds more easily.
descriptions.heroin: An opioid made from morphine, sold as a white or brown powder or as black tar. It relieves pain, brings on heavy sedation, and slows breathing. Across much of the US, what is sold as heroin now has fentanyl in it, or is fentanyl. Strength can change from one batch to the next.
descriptions.fentanyl: A synthetic opioid used in hospitals for severe pain, and now the main opioid in the US street supply. It relieves pain and slows breathing like other opioids. It works in far smaller amounts than heroin, so it is very hard to mix evenly. Two scoops from the same bag can be different strengths.
descriptions.methamphetamine: A strong stimulant, sold as a crystal or a powder. It brings energy, focus and confidence, and it lasts far longer than cocaine. Heavy or long-term use is linked to lost sleep and weight, tooth damage, and paranoia or psychosis that can last after you stop.
descriptions.amphetamine: A stimulant, prescribed as Adderall for ADHD and also used without a prescription. It sharpens focus, gives you energy, keeps you awake and kills appetite. The prescribed and street versions are the same drug — the difference is that a prescription comes with a known strength.
descriptions.methylphenidate: A stimulant prescribed as Ritalin or Concerta, mostly for ADHD. It sharpens focus and gives you energy, and does not last as long as amphetamine.
descriptions.alprazolam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Xanax for anxiety and panic. It calms and sedates, and it interferes with laying down memories of the hours it is active. Pressed pills sold as Xanax frequently contain a different benzodiazepine, or none at all.
descriptions.diazepam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Valium for anxiety, muscle spasm and alcohol withdrawal. It sedates, relaxes muscle and lowers anxiety. It lasts longer than most of its family: what the body breaks it down into keeps working for a day or more.
descriptions.oxycodone: An opioid painkiller, prescribed as OxyContin or Percocet. It kills pain, sedates you and brings euphoria. Pills sold as oxycodone outside a pharmacy — especially ones stamped M30 — are very often pressed fentanyl instead.
descriptions.codeine: A weaker opioid, in some prescription cough syrups and pain tablets. Your body turns it into morphine. How much it turns varies a lot from person to person, so the same tablet hits two people differently.
descriptions.buprenorphine: An opioid used to treat opioid dependence and pain, prescribed as Suboxone or Subutex. It sits on the same receptors without doing the same thing, which takes away withdrawal and cravings. Because it grips those receptors so tightly, taking it too soon after another opioid can throw you straight into withdrawal.
descriptions.tramadol: A prescription painkiller. It works partly as a weak opioid and partly on serotonin and norepinephrine, the way some antidepressants do. That second part is why it reacts badly with antidepressants and raises the chance of a seizure.
descriptions.kratom: The leaf of a Southeast Asian tree, taken as powder, capsules or tea. Smaller amounts feel more like a stimulant, larger amounts more like a mild opioid. Some people use it for pain, or to get through opioid withdrawal. Using it regularly can build dependence, with a withdrawal of its own.
descriptions.ghb: A depressant sold as a salty liquid, used recreationally and sometimes for sleep. It sedates and disinhibits, and the amount that produces those effects and the amount that produces unconsciousness are very close together. It occurs naturally in the body in tiny amounts, and GBL converts into it after swallowing.
descriptions.dmt: A very short, very intense psychedelic, usually smoked or vaped. It arrives within seconds and is usually over in fifteen to thirty minutes. It is also what makes ayahuasca work. With an MAOI it lasts hours instead. That combination reacts badly with a lot of medications.
descriptions.mescaline: A psychedelic found in peyote, San Pedro and related cacti, used in Indigenous ceremony for a very long time. Visual and emotional changes lasting roughly ten to twelve hours. Peyote grows slowly and is under threat, and its ceremonial use is legally protected for members of the Native American Church.
descriptions.2c-b: A synthetic psychedelic with a stimulant edge, sold as pills or powder. Shorter than LSD — usually four to eight hours. It belongs to a family of near-identical chemicals with very different strengths. Mixing one up for another is the usual way people get hurt with it.
descriptions.nitrous: Nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, used by dentists and to charge whipped cream canisters. Breathed in, you get about a minute of dizziness and distortion. Two specific dangers. Breathing it without oxygen can suffocate you. Using a lot of it strips out your vitamin B12, which causes nerve damage.
descriptions.pregabalin: A prescription medicine for nerve pain, seizures and anxiety, sold as Lyrica. It is a depressant: calming, sedating, and at higher doses euphoric. It works on calcium channels in nerve cells rather than on the benzodiazepine or opioid systems.
descriptions.gabapentin: A prescription medicine for nerve pain and seizures, sold as Neurontin. Like pregabalin it sedates you and stacks with opioids and alcohol. People tend to assume it is harmless because it is everywhere and handed out freely.
descriptions.methadone: An opioid used both to treat opioid dependence and for pain. It relieves pain and withdrawal without the sharp peak of heroin or fentanyl. It also lasts far longer than either, often more than a day. Because it clears slowly, it accumulates over the first few days of regular dosing before levelling off.
descriptions.morphine: The original opioid painkiller, made from the opium poppy and still used in hospitals for severe pain. Nearly every other opioid gets measured against it.
descriptions.hydrocodone: An opioid painkiller, prescribed as Vicodin or Norco, usually mixed with acetaminophen. That mix matters: taking extra tablets to get more opioid also means more acetaminophen, and acetaminophen wrecks your liver.
descriptions.hydromorphone: A strong opioid painkiller, prescribed as Dilaudid, used in hospitals for severe pain. A good deal stronger than morphine, milligram for milligram.
descriptions.oxymorphone: A strong opioid painkiller, prescribed as Opana. Stronger than oxycodone, milligram for milligram.
descriptions.tapentadol: A prescription painkiller that acts both as an opioid and on norepinephrine, in a single molecule. The opioid action relieves pain; the second action is the same mechanism some antidepressants use.
descriptions.pethidine: An older opioid painkiller, also called meperidine or Demerol, once common in childbirth and surgery. Used far less now, because something it breaks down into builds up with repeated doses and can cause seizures.
descriptions.dihydrocodeine: An opioid painkiller about as strong as codeine, found in some prescription tablets and cough medicines.
descriptions.o-desmethyltramadol: What the body turns tramadol into, and the part that actually relieves pain. It is sometimes sold on its own, including in products marketed as herbal, at strengths that are not stated.
descriptions.dextropropoxyphene: An opioid painkiller, pulled from the US and much of Europe. It caused heart rhythm problems at amounts not far above a normal dose.
descriptions.acetylfentanyl: A fentanyl analogue — a chemical cousin of fentanyl. It was never made as a medicine and turns up in the street opioid supply. Like fentanyl, it works in tiny amounts, so it is hard to mix evenly.
descriptions.sufentanil: A hospital opioid, used in surgery and epidurals. It relieves pain and sedates like other opioids. By weight it is far stronger than fentanyl, working in the low microgram range.
descriptions.u-47700: A synthetic opioid, sometimes sold as pink or U4. It was made for research and never approved as a medicine. It shows up as a powder, or pressed into fake pills.
descriptions.dextromethorphan: The cough suppressant in many over-the-counter cold medicines, often labeled DXM. At ordinary doses it suppresses coughing; at much larger ones it acts as a dissociative, producing detachment and altered perception. Cold medicines often combine it with acetaminophen or antihistamines, which are different drugs with their own effects.
descriptions.pcp: A dissociative anesthetic, also called angel dust, dropped from medical use because of how confused and agitated people were as it wore off. It leaves you detached from your body and your surroundings, and does unpredictable things to mood and behavior.
descriptions.mephedrone: A stimulant, also called 4-MMC or meow meow, sold as powder or in capsules. Energy and sociability for a short time, which is exactly why people redose.
descriptions.3-mmc: A stimulant closely related to mephedrone, sold after mephedrone got banned in a lot of countries. Similar effects, similarly short.
descriptions.a-pvp: A stimulant that lasts a long time, sometimes called flakka, part of the cathinone family. Effects can run for many hours, and at higher amounts it brings agitation, sleeplessness and confusion.
descriptions.methylone: A stimulant with a mild emotional edge, chemically related to MDMA but much weaker on that front. It has been sold as MDMA, and mixed into things labeled MDMA.
descriptions.mda: A psychedelic stimulant closely related to MDMA, sometimes called sally. Lasts longer than MDMA, with more visual effect and less of the emotional warmth.
descriptions.mdea: A drug closely related to MDMA, sometimes called eve, with a milder emotional effect.
descriptions.gbl: An industrial solvent that the body turns into GHB after you swallow it. The effects are the same as GHB's. So is the small gap between the amount that gets you high and the amount that puts you out.
descriptions.baclofen: A prescription muscle relaxant for spasticity, sometimes used for alcohol dependence. It is a depressant and adds to what opioids and alcohol are already doing. Stopping it suddenly after regular use can cause serious withdrawal.
descriptions.mdai: A drug related to MDMA that brings emotional warmth without much stimulation. Sometimes sold as a legal stand-in for MDMA.
descriptions.5-apb: A stimulant with a psychedelic edge, sold as an MDMA substitute, and often lasting a lot longer than people expect.
descriptions.6-apb: A stimulant with a psychedelic edge, sometimes called benzo fury, sold as an MDMA substitute. It comes on slowly, which is how people end up taking more than they meant to. Then it lasts a long time.
descriptions.caffeine: The stimulant in coffee, tea and energy drinks, and a very common cutting agent in powders sold as something else. On its own it is mild; mixed into a stimulant it makes a bag look bigger without making it stronger.
descriptions.nicotine: The drug in tobacco and vapes. It is a stimulant: it sharpens attention briefly, raises heart rate, and builds dependence faster than almost anything else here. It acts on the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, which is where the name comes from.
descriptions.clonazepam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Klonopin for seizures and panic. Long-acting. Like the rest of its family it stacks with opioids and alcohol, and stopping suddenly after regular use can cause seizures.
descriptions.lorazepam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Ativan for anxiety and seizures. Shorter-acting than diazepam. Same two rules as the rest of the family. It stacks with opioids and alcohol. Coming off it has to be gradual.
descriptions.zolpidem: A sleeping pill, prescribed as Ambien. It brings on sleep quickly and wears off fast. It is not a benzodiazepine, but it works on the same GABA-A system. It is known for people doing things while apparently awake and not remembering afterwards.
descriptions.zopiclone: A sleeping pill, sold as Imovane or Zimovane. Like zolpidem it is not a benzodiazepine but acts on the same GABA-A system. It commonly leaves a metallic taste in the mouth.
descriptions.eszopiclone: A sleeping pill, prescribed as Lunesta. Closely related to zopiclone and carries the same warning about mixing with opioids or alcohol.
descriptions.etizolam: A benzodiazepine-type drug — a thienodiazepine — prescribed in a few countries and sold widely online everywhere else. It sedates and reduces anxiety like the rest of the family. It is often what is actually in a pill sold as Xanax, and strength varies enormously batch to batch.
descriptions.flualprazolam: A designer benzodiazepine, never a medicine anywhere. It turns up pressed into fake Xanax, and it is much stronger than alprazolam. So a pill that looks familiar can be far more sedating than expected.
descriptions.flubromazolam: A designer benzodiazepine, never approved as a medicine. Very strong in very small amounts and long-lasting, which is a bad combination when nobody knows how much is in a pill.
descriptions.metizolam: A designer benzodiazepine sold online, never a medicine. Like the others in this group, the real problem is that the amount in any given pill is unknown.
descriptions.deschloroetizolam: A designer benzodiazepine related to etizolam, never approved as a medicine and not made to any consistent strength.
descriptions.phenibut: A Russian anxiety medicine sold as a supplement in the US. It is a depressant and adds to alcohol and opioids. Dependence builds faster than people expect, and the withdrawal is genuinely severe — closer to benzodiazepine withdrawal than to a hangover.
descriptions.f-phenibut: A stronger, faster version of phenibut, sold as a supplement. Same dependence and same severe withdrawal, reached sooner.
descriptions.modafinil: A prescription wakefulness drug, sold as Provigil, used for narcolepsy and shift work. It keeps you awake without much of a stimulant rush. It speeds up how the liver clears some medicines, which matters most for hormonal birth control.
descriptions.armodafinil: A longer-lasting version of modafinil, prescribed as Nuvigil, with the same effects and the same interaction with hormonal birth control.
descriptions.psilocin: What your body turns psilocybin into, and the part that actually does something. It is also what is measured when mushrooms are tested.
descriptions.datura: A plant — jimsonweed or thornapple — containing deliriants. This is not a psychedelic: people experience convincing hallucinations they cannot tell from real, often with no memory afterwards. The amount varies wildly between plants, and even between parts of the same plant. The gap between an active dose and a poisonous one is small.
descriptions.ayahuasca: A brew from South America combining a DMT-containing plant with an MAOI plant, traditionally used in ceremony. The MAOI is what makes it last hours rather than minutes. It is also the part that reacts badly with many antidepressants and with some foods.
descriptions.changa: DMT absorbed onto an herb blend that includes an MAOI, made to be smoked. It lasts longer than smoked DMT alone, and the MAOI brings the same medication interactions ayahuasca has.
descriptions.melatonin: A hormone the brain makes at night to time sleep. The version sold in shops is a supplement, taken to fall asleep or to reset after a time-zone change. It is not a sedative and does not knock you out: it shifts when you feel sleepy rather than forcing it.
descriptions.myristicin: A compound in nutmeg, and the reason large amounts of the spice affect people. Swallowing a lot of it is well documented as unpleasant: hours of nausea, a racing heart, dry mouth and confusion. It comes on slowly and can last a day or more.
descriptions.diphenhydramine: The antihistamine in Benadryl and many night-time cold medicines. It causes drowsiness at normal doses. At high doses it is a deliriant: confusion and hallucinations that people find frightening. It also adds to the sedation of anything else that slows you down.
descriptions.cannabidiol: CBD — a compound from the cannabis plant sold in oils, drinks and gummies. It does not get you high the way THC does. It is sold for anxiety, pain and sleep. The evidence for that is thin. The exception is two rare seizure disorders, where a prescription version works well. Products vary wildly in what they actually contain.
descriptions.kava: A drink made from the root of a Pacific Islands plant. It is traditional in Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga and Samoa. In the US it is sold in kava bars and as capsules. It relaxes the body and calms without clouding thinking much.
descriptions.blue-lotus: A water lily used in ancient Egyptian art and ritual, sold now as a tea, a vape or a tincture. People report mild calm and drowsiness. Almost none of it has been studied properly, so what it does at the amounts people take is not established.
descriptions.creatine: A sports supplement, one of the most studied there is. It helps muscles produce short bursts of power, so people take it for strength training. It is not psychoactive — it is here because it turns up in stacks alongside things that are.
descriptions.theanine: An amino acid found in tea leaves, sold as a supplement and often paired with caffeine. People take it to take the edge off caffeine's jitteriness. Effects are mild; it is here because it is a common ingredient in energy and "focus" products.
descriptions.theacrine: A compound related to caffeine, found in kucha tea and sold in energy and pre-workout products. It is stimulating and appears to build less tolerance than caffeine. Human research on it is limited.
descriptions.alpha-gpc: A choline supplement sold for memory and focus, and used in some countries as a prescription drug after a stroke. It is a building block your body uses to make a brain chemical involved in attention. Sold over the counter in the US as a nootropic.
descriptions.choline-bitartrate: A cheap, common form of choline, an essential nutrient found in eggs and liver. Sold as a supplement for memory and often taken alongside nootropics. Little of it reaches the brain compared with the other forms sold for the same purpose.
descriptions.citicoline: A choline supplement sold for memory and attention. In parts of Europe and Asia it is a prescription medicine, given after strokes and head injuries. Sold over the counter in the US.
descriptions.n-acetylcysteine: NAC — a supplement, and also a hospital medicine, where it is the antidote for acetaminophen poisoning. It is a precursor to glutathione, one of the body's own antioxidants. Over the counter it is sold for the lungs, the liver, and on thinner evidence for cravings.
descriptions.sam-e: A supplement sold for mood and joints, and a prescription antidepressant in several European countries. It is a substance the body already makes, used in reactions all over the body. It acts on the same serotonin system antidepressants do.
descriptions.tyrosine: An amino acid from ordinary protein in food, sold as a supplement. Your body uses it to build dopamine and adrenaline, which is why it is marketed for focus and for performing under stress. Effects in well-rested people are small.
descriptions.5-hydroxytryptophan: 5-HTP — a supplement the body converts directly into serotonin, sold for mood and sleep. It is the intermediate step between tryptophan and serotonin, which is why it raises serotonin levels rather than acting on a receptor itself.
descriptions.galantamine: A prescription medicine for Alzheimer's disease, derived from snowdrops, and sold as a supplement for lucid dreaming. It raises levels of a brain chemical involved in memory.
descriptions.naloxone: The overdose-reversal drug, sold as Narcan and as a generic nasal spray or injection. It knocks opioids off their receptors and restores breathing, usually within a few minutes. It has no effect on a person with no opioids in them. It wears off in 30 to 90 minutes, sooner than most opioids do.
descriptions.clonidine: A blood-pressure medicine also prescribed for ADHD, anxiety, hot flushes and — commonly — to take the edge off opioid withdrawal. It lowers blood pressure and heart rate, so it can cause fainting, and it stacks with anything else that sedates.
descriptions.promethazine: A prescription antihistamine used for nausea, allergies and as a sedative, and the other half of "lean" when mixed with codeine cough syrup. It is heavily sedating on its own and adds to the breathing suppression of opioids.
descriptions.prochlorperazine: A prescription medicine for severe nausea, vomiting and vertigo. It is sedating, and it can cause distressing muscle stiffness and restlessness in a minority of people who take it.
descriptions.quetiapine: An antipsychotic sold as Seroquel, prescribed for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and very widely prescribed off-label at low doses as a sleeping aid. Strongly sedating.
descriptions.mirtazapine: An antidepressant also prescribed for sleep and appetite. It is sedating, most noticeably at lower doses, and it increases appetite. It acts on serotonin and norepinephrine receptors rather than by blocking reuptake the way SSRIs do.
descriptions.risperidone: An antipsychotic prescribed for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and irritability in autism. Sometimes given in emergency rooms to somebody in a drug-induced psychosis.
descriptions.haloperidol: An older antipsychotic, best known as the drug given by injection in emergency rooms to calm somebody agitated or psychotic. It can cause severe muscle stiffness and restlessness.
descriptions.ephedrine: A stimulant from the ephedra plant. In the US it is sold over the counter for congestion and asthma. It raises heart rate and blood pressure. Sales are tracked, because it can be used to make methamphetamine.
descriptions.benzydamine: An anti-inflammatory sold over the counter in many countries as a throat spray, gargle or lozenge for mouth and throat pain. Swallowed in large amounts it causes hallucinations and agitation, which is the only reason it appears here.
descriptions.carisoprodol: A muscle relaxant, prescribed as Soma. It sedates and relaxes muscle. The body turns part of it into meprobamate, an old sedative. That is why it is habit-forming, and why it stacks with opioids and alcohol.
descriptions.tizanidine: A prescription muscle relaxant for spasms and spasticity. It lowers blood pressure and is sedating.
descriptions.progesterone: A hormone your body makes, also prescribed as a medicine in hormone therapy, contraception and fertility treatment. It is on this list because it changes how the body handles some other drugs, not because it is taken to get high.
descriptions.lisdexamfetamine: Vyvanse — a prescription stimulant for ADHD and binge-eating disorder. It does nothing until your body turns it into dexamfetamine. That is why it comes on slowly, and why it is harder to misuse than other amphetamine pills.
descriptions.dextroamphetamine: A prescription stimulant for ADHD and narcolepsy, and the more active half of Adderall. It increases alertness, focus and heart rate.
descriptions.memantine: A prescription medicine for moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease. It acts on the same receptor as ketamine but far more weakly and much more slowly, and it is not sedating.
descriptions.piracetam: The original "nootropic" — the word was coined for it. Sold as a supplement in the US and prescribed in parts of Europe for cognitive decline and involuntary muscle jerks. Evidence in healthy people is weak.
descriptions.aniracetam: A nootropic in the same family as piracetam, sold as a supplement in the US and as a prescription medicine in some countries. Marketed for memory and anxiety; human evidence is limited.
descriptions.oxiracetam: A nootropic in the piracetam family, sold as a supplement and marketed for memory and focus. Studied mostly in cognitive decline rather than in healthy people.
descriptions.pramiracetam: A nootropic in the piracetam family, sold as a supplement. Marketed for memory; the small amount of research on it is in brain injury, not in healthy people.
descriptions.phenylpiracetam: A nootropic in the piracetam family developed in the Soviet space program, sold as a supplement. Unlike the others it is noticeably stimulating, and it is banned in competitive sport for that reason.
descriptions.adrafinil: A supplement your liver converts into modafinil, the prescription wakefulness drug. It is sold over the counter in the US because it is not itself a controlled substance. The conversion is hard on the liver, which is the main reason to know what it is.
descriptions.methaqualone: Quaaludes — a sedative widely prescribed for sleep in the 1960s and 70s, then banned almost everywhere after widespread misuse. It is essentially absent from the modern supply; pills sold under the name today are usually something else.
descriptions.lsa: The psychedelic compound in morning glory and Hawaiian baby woodrose seeds, which people eat for a long, dreamy, often nauseating experience. Seeds sold for planting are frequently coated with fungicides, and the nausea and vomiting are close to universal.
descriptions.grayanotoxin: A toxin in rhododendron and related plants, which turns up in honey made from their nectar. A small amount causes tingling and light-headedness. A little more drops heart rate and blood pressure hard enough to put people in hospital.
descriptions.salvinorin-a: The active compound in salvia divinorum, a sage plant, usually smoked as dried leaf. It produces an intense, disorienting experience that is over in minutes and that many people find frightening rather than pleasant. It is not related to any other psychedelic.
descriptions.ibogaine: A compound from the iboga shrub. It is used in Bwiti ceremonies in Gabon, and taken in unregulated clinics abroad to interrupt opioid dependence. It is not approved anywhere in the US. It disturbs heart rhythm, and accidents in clinic settings are documented. It is sold as a supervised medical treatment. It is not one.
descriptions.inhalants: A category rather than one drug: solvents, glues, aerosols, nitrous oxide, and the alkyl nitrites sold as poppers. What they share is being breathed in for a short high. What they do to the body differs completely between them, and some can stop the heart on a first use.
descriptions.phenobarbital: An old barbiturate, still prescribed for epilepsy and used in hospitals to manage severe alcohol withdrawal. It is a long-acting sedative. It works on the GABA-A receptor, holding the channel open itself. Benzodiazepines only boost the body's own signal, which is the difference between the two.
descriptions.pentobarbital: A barbiturate once prescribed for sleep, now used mainly in hospitals for anesthesia and seizures, and in veterinary euthanasia. Like all barbiturates it suppresses breathing and the safety margin is narrow.
descriptions.secobarbital: A barbiturate sleeping pill, widely prescribed decades ago and rare now. It suppresses breathing, and mixing it with alcohol is what made it notorious.
descriptions.flunitrazepam: Rohypnol — a strong benzodiazepine sleeping pill, prescribed in some countries and never approved in the US. It sedates heavily and interferes with memory formation. It is known mainly for drink spiking, and the manufacturer added a blue dye that colors a drink for that reason.
descriptions.midazolam: A short-acting benzodiazepine given in hospitals for sedation before procedures, and to stop prolonged seizures. It works fast and reliably erases memory of the procedure, which is intentional.
descriptions.temazepam: A benzodiazepine prescribed for sleep. Like all benzodiazepines it suppresses breathing alongside opioids and alcohol, and stopping it suddenly after regular use can cause seizures.
descriptions.bromazepam: A benzodiazepine prescribed for anxiety in many countries, though not in the US. It reduces anxiety and sedates, in the middle of its family for how long it lasts.

education.intro: Nobody is born knowing how to reverse an overdose. These are free, short, and designed for people with no medical background — and some of them come with naloxone in the box at the end.

groups.title: Overdose response and naloxone
groups.blurb: The one to do first. Most take under an hour, several are free and mail you naloxone.

items.name: End Overdose
items.what: Free online certification in opioid overdose response. Their opioid course lists a certificate of completion and a free naloxone kit as what you get for finishing — training and supply in one step. There is also a short game-based version.

items.name: GetNaloxoneNow
items.what: Free online overdose response training, widely used by health departments and often the course a state program points you at.

items.name: NEXT Distro
items.what: Mail-based naloxone. Most states require you to complete their short online training before they ship — that is the norm for free-by-mail programs, not an obstacle they invented.

items.what: In-person training, usually same-day naloxone, and people who can answer questions a website cannot. Often the fastest route if there is one near you.

groups.blurb: Worth having for the overdose where there is no pulse — and for everything else in a life.

why.title: Do you need training to use naloxone?
why.body: Legally, no — naloxone nasal spray is available over the counter nationwide and you can use it on someone without any certification. Practically, training matters: it is the difference between knowing the steps and working them out while someone is not breathing. It also covers what naloxone does not fix, which is where people get caught out.
why.note: Many free-naloxone programs do ask you to complete a short course before they ship. That is how the supply is funded and tracked — worth doing early rather than on the night you need it.

beforeTheNight.headline: Long nights and hot days
beforeTheNight.blurb: The two that catch people out at an event, before the night rather than during it.

items.t: Overheating, and over-drinking
items.d: Dancing in a hot room you can lose about a pint of water an hour, and stimulants make overheating more likely. Two to three cups an hour — about half a liter — is the ceiling while you are actually dancing, not a target, because past that the water dilutes the sodium in your blood until the brain starts to swell, and at events MDMA is the reason that happens so often. Eat something; food is what keeps your electrolytes where they should be.
items.note: Heat stroke is not the one where they stop sweating — that is the heat wave kind. Somebody having one on a dancefloor is usually still pouring sweat. What tells you is that they stop making sense.

harm._doc: Harm between people: accountability after a mistake, abuse (yours or someone you know), and public allegations from all three seats. Every item carries a source that was fetched and read; anything the sources did not support was left out rather than guessed. Do not edit prose here without re-reading the cited source. Sections render on Learn beside consent.json.

accountability.title: Staying accountable
accountability.intro: The apology is the short part. Accountability is what you keep doing when nobody is making you. A lot of it happens away from the person you hurt. This is that part.

callout.title: If it is still happening, stop first
callout.body: It is very hard to take responsibility for harm that is still going on. So the toolkit's first step is to stop it.

groups.title: What it is, and what it is not

items.t: It starts with you, and sooner is better
items.d: Accountability is your own job. It is not something you wait to be made to do. The essay behind the four parts was written for small hurts and breaks in trust. For those, it says to say something as soon as you know you did it. Before they have to raise it. Waiting risks letting the hurt harden into resentment. They start building their own story, sometimes that it was their fault. You start building yours, that it was not that bad or it is too late. Needing to prepare first is often an excuse. The window for an apology can close.

sources.name: Mia Mingus — the four parts of accountability

items.t: It does not mean you get forgiven
items.d: The person you hurt does not have to forgive you. An apology does not settle it. The relationship does not have to continue. You may never be trusted again. They can always refuse an apology. They may not feel safe refusing it to your face. Someone who still feels in danger from you is not in a place to forgive. The Hotline says the path to forgiveness usually includes some accountability or changed behavior.

sources.name: Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)
National Domestic Violence Hotline — if an abusive partner apologizes

items.t: Sorry with a but is not sorry
items.d: Sorry, but you should not have made me angry, is not an apology. Sorry, but I never saw a healthy relationship, is not one either. The National Domestic Violence Hotline has a checklist of signs you may be hurting a partner. Blaming your anger on drugs, alcohol or the other person is on it. The toolkit's version is the same. Recognize the consequences without excuses, even where you did not intend them. What you did was a choice, not something someone else caused. Words have to match actions. A real apology does not end at the word sorry. Repeated sorries followed by the same behavior wear down trust. They wear down hope that anything will change.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — if an abusive partner apologizes
National Domestic Violence Hotline — am I hurting my partner?
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

items.t: Feeling defensive is expected
items.d: Thoughts like it is none of their business, or what about my side, are expected. The toolkit's advice is to slow down. To notice you are not going to be destroyed. It names the usual reactions: attacking back, withdrawing completely, or building your own camp of supporters. It says to find someone who supports you and challenges you at the same time. Someone who only agrees you were right is not that person.

sources.name: Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

items.t: The four exits from shame
items.d: One research model names four ways people cope with shame. Attack yourself. Withdraw. Avoid or minimize. Attack others. It names a fifth, and calls it adaptive: admitting it and moving to apologize or make amends. Shame pushes people to hide, and to get angry and blame others. Guilt points the other way, toward owning it and undoing the damage. The model is a way to see which one you are doing right now.

sources.name: Tangney et al., Annual Review of Psychology (2007)

items.t: Which part was actually yours
items.d: Guilt about a specific thing has ways out. Change the behavior. Repair the damage. Apologize. If none of those is possible, resolve to do better. Guilt about a clear wrong is not linked to depression or anxiety on its own. It gets there when it spreads into shame about your whole self. It also gets there when you take on blame for things outside your control. So part of the work is being exact about what was actually yours. Not more, not less.

sources.name: Tangney et al., Annual Review of Psychology (2007)

items.t: Support has to come from someone other than the person you hurt
items.d: Changing what you do is the hardest part. It is easier with help. The essay's advice is to find people now. People you can talk to about your mistakes, shame and guilt. Before anyone calls you on anything. Harmful behavior is often part of a bigger pattern. A pattern takes more than fixing one thing. The person you hurt does not carry your accountability. Telling other people what you did counts as accountability in itself. Not to gather sympathizers. To stop hiding it, and to ask for help changing.

sources.name: Mia Mingus — the four parts of accountability
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

items.t: The ways people slip out of it
items.d: The toolkit lists the common ones. Leaving the community or relationship to avoid it. Changing early, then sliding back once the pressure drops. Hoping people forget. Hoping people feel sorry for you. Blaming your past. Blaming the person you hurt. Making the process itself the problem. Insisting your version of accountability is the right one. It is a list to check yourself against.

sources.name: Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

items.t: What real change looks like
items.d: The National Domestic Violence Hotline lists signs that an abusive partner is making real progress. Admitting fully. Dropping excuses and blame. Making amends. Not asking for credit for improvements. Not treating improvements as vouchers to spend on occasional acts of abuse. Not declaring yourself cured. Accepting consequences without self-pity or blaming others.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — is change possible in an abuser?

items.t: Some of it is not yours to control
items.d: Repair happens in relationship. You cannot do it alone. Sometimes it is not possible, because they do not want to engage with you. Seeing what you did, and changing, are still yours to do. If repair does happen, they choose how involved they are. From leading it to not being there at all. Your idea of what would fix it and theirs may differ. Some things cannot be given back. One of the toolkit's affirmations: offer the apology as a gift, expecting nothing back. Losing respect, standing, relationships, sometimes a home or a community, are possible costs of harm. The toolkit calls them costs, not punishments. Eventually you accept the losses you cannot control, and build self-respect anyway. If you share a community but were not close, the goal may be smaller. Just being in the same space without conflict.

sources.name: Mia Mingus — the four parts of accountability
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

notThis.title: Not a program that skips the point
notThis.body: If this was a pattern with a partner, the National Domestic Violence Hotline is specific. On their own, it does not recommend couples counseling or anger management. Nor substance-use programs or mental health treatment. It says they can sit alongside a certified batterer intervention program. The Hotline takes calls from people who think they may be causing harm. Not only from people being hurt. It says acknowledging it now is the first step. The number is under Survivors of abuse and violence in Communities.

abuse.title: When the person hurting you is someone close
abuse.intro: Some people are controlled through what they use. That has a name, and there are people who work on it. Nothing here tells you to leave. It is about seeing what is happening. Staying safer where you are. What to do if it is a friend.

callout.title: The drugs are not the reason
callout.body: Abuse is about power and control. Drugs are not the root cause. Getting sober does not by itself end it.

groups.title: What it looks like when drugs are part of it

items.t: Abuse is a pattern, not one bad night
items.d: It is one person keeping power and control over another. Hitting is only part of it. Threats, put-downs, control of money, being kept from friends and family. These usually come together. Early on the person can seem ideal, and the signs grow over time. Some from the National Domestic Violence Hotline's list: being told you never do anything right. Extreme jealousy about your time away. Being shamed in front of others. Pressure for sex. Pressure to use. Threats to kids or pets. Your things destroyed. Even one or two is a red flag. Anyone can be on either side of this.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — understand relationship abuse
National Domestic Violence Hotline — warning signs of abuse

items.t: Being made to use is part of it
items.d: NCDVTMH calls it substance use coercion. Its own list: being made to use, or use more than you wanted. Someone controlling your supply. Being put into withdrawal to get you to do something. Being stopped from cutting down or quitting. Being kept from a meeting or treatment. Being told you would be arrested, or lose your kids, if you called the police. Being told an assault was your fault because you were high. A yes to any one of these may mean it is happening to you. NCDVTMH also says this is not uncommon. A partner gets you onto opioids, then controls the supply. Then come threats if you try to cut down, get treatment, or call the police. Withdrawal, jail, losing your kids, or violence. Abusers lean on the shame around use to keep control.

sources.name: NCDVTMH — mental health and substance abuse coercion tipsheet (PDF)
NCDVTMH — substance use coercion, opioids, and domestic violence

items.t: It is common enough that people have counted
items.d: In 2012 the Hotline surveyed about 3,000 women who called. 27% said a partner had pressured or forced them to use, or to use more. Some had tried to get help for their use. Of those, 60% said a partner had tried to stop or discourage them. That was Hotline callers, and women only. It does not say how common this is for everyone. It does say you are not the only one.

sources.name: NCDVTMH and National Domestic Violence Hotline — mental health and substance use coercion surveys report, 2014 (PDF)

items.t: The calm after is part of the pattern
items.d: After a blowup there is often a stretch of apologies and promises. The person seems perfect for a while. The Hotline calls that a tactic. It keeps you there and makes you doubt it was really that bad. Gaslighting works the same way. It makes you question what you know happened.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — supporting someone who keeps returning

groups.title: Staying safer while you are still there

items.t: A plan is for staying, not only for leaving
items.d: You do not have to be going anywhere to make one. The Hotline says planning matters more when you live with the person. You cannot just walk out. Its advocates will build one around your situation, by phone or chat, any hour. The number and text line are in Communities, under Survivors of abuse and violence.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — safety planning while living with an abusive partner
National Domestic Violence Hotline — create your personal safety plan

items.t: Things nobody else has to know about
items.d: The Hotline's list for people still at home. Notice how much force they use. It helps you judge the danger before it comes. Know which rooms have a way out and no weapons. Move there when an argument builds. Keep a phone within reach and know who you would call. Lock guns and knives away if you can. Have a few ordinary reasons ready for leaving the house. Keep the car backed in and fueled. Write down what happens. Decide now what you will do if it is found. If they have ever put hands around your neck, skip scarves and jewelry. Those can be used against you. If violence cannot be avoided, get to a corner. Make yourself small. Cover your head with your arms.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — safety planning while living with an abusive partner

items.t: Let one or two people in
items.d: Tell a friend or neighbor you trust. Agree a signal they can see that means you need help. Tell them plainly who to call in a crisis, and who not to. Include whether you want the police. If kids or roommates are there, talk about how they get help. Agree a signal with them too. Ask them to stay out of the violence itself.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — safety planning while living with an abusive partner

items.t: Your head is part of the plan
items.d: Keep people around who are good to you. Pick one small step, like calling an advocate, with no promise to do anything after. Have a place that feels calm. If you keep a journal, keep it where they cannot get to it. It is not your fault. You do not have to decide everything at once.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — planning for emotional safety

groups.title: If it is someone you know

items.t: Ask, do not decide for them
items.d: Ask how you can help, instead of guessing. They know their partner, and what keeps them and you safe. Their partner already ignores what they want. One more person deciding for them does not help. The Hotline says not to stage an intervention. Ultimatums, calling the police, or trying to pull someone out can add danger. Heavy pressure can also mean they stop coming to you. That is what the abuser wants. Leaving and going back more than once is common. You cannot save another person. What helps: a place to talk without judgment. Ordinary time together. Being there whether they stay, go, or go back. You can say you are at your limit and point them to the Hotline.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — when a survivor asks you for help
National Domestic Violence Hotline — so you want to stage an intervention
National Domestic Violence Hotline — can I save them?
National Domestic Violence Hotline — supporting someone who keeps returning

items.t: Calling the police for them is not always safer
items.d: The Hotline says calling without their agreement takes away their say over their own safety. They may not feel safe being honest with officers, especially with the abuser there. Officers may not see what is happening. The abuser may hurt them more after the police leave. It is riskier still if the abuser has ties to the department. Immediate physical danger is different. Otherwise: ask privately what they need. Write down what you see, with dates and times. You can also contact a Hotline advocate to think through safety planning. A neighbor knocking on the door can interrupt.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — should I call the police for someone else?
National Domestic Violence Hotline — when a survivor asks you for help

items.t: If someone tells you they were assaulted
items.d: RAINN's guide. Thank them for telling you. Ask what would help most right now. Listen without shock, blame, or why questions. Say you believe them and it was not their fault, as often as needed. Do not ask what they were wearing, or whether they had been drinking. Do not ask why they did not fight back. Or why they did not tell someone sooner. Never push them to report or get an exam. If they want a doctor or the police, offer to go with them. Keep checking in over time. There is no timeline for this. Your own feelings about it go to someone else, not to them.

sources.name: RAINN — how to TALK with survivors of sexual violence

notThis.title: Not a plan for leaving, and not legal advice
notThis.body: The Hotline says it plainly. The person in it has the right to decide if, when, and how they leave. Protective orders and custody differ by state. A lawyer or legal aid can tell you what applies where you are.

accused.title: If someone says you hurt them
accused.intro: Someone has said you hurt them. In person, in a group chat, or in public. This is what people who work on harm say about the first hours and after. It cannot tell you whether it is true. Nobody here can. The first steps are the same either way.

callout.title: Do not reach out to the person who named you
callout.body: They decide if there is any contact and when, and asking twice is pressure.

items.t: Stop before you answer anyone
items.d: You will feel a lot right now. Worry, guilt, shame, anger, the urge to defend yourself. All of that is normal. Take time before you reply to anyone. The pause is there so the feelings do not do more damage.

sources.name: DanceSafe — responding to and repairing a consent violation
DanceSafe — power dynamics, accountability and community response

items.t: Do not contact the person who named you
items.d: They decide whether there is any contact, and when. Not you. If you already asked and they said no, it stays no until they say otherwise. Asking again is pressure. Whether there is ever a conversation is theirs to decide.

sources.name: TransformHarm — suggestions to people called out for abusive behavior (Clamor, 2002)
TransformHarm — 9 ways to be accountable when you have been abusive (Everyday Feminism, 2016)

items.t: Do not post your side
items.d: No rebuttal in the group chat. No list of what they got wrong. No saying they are lying, or asking why they are doing this now. That kind of reply tells everyone else who has been hurt to stay quiet. If you say anything, keep to what you remember of your own actions. Put the rest on a therapist, or someone completely outside the scene. If you are sure it is not true, that does not change the first days. One of these guides was written by someone who was named. Months later they were told the claim had no basis. They still say the same thing. No contact. No rebuttal. The needs of the person naming you come first.

sources.name: TransformHarm — suggestions to people called out for abusive behavior (Clamor, 2002)

items.t: Friends vouching for you does not help
items.d: People who love you will want to defend your character. Ask them not to. Ask them to help you look at what you did instead. Look for someone who can support you and challenge you at the same time. Not someone who only agrees that you were right. If you already have people like that, this is what they are for.

sources.name: TransformHarm — suggestions to people called out for abusive behavior (Clamor, 2002)
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)
Mia Mingus — the four parts of accountability

groups.title: What it does to your head

items.t: Feeling attacked is the usual first reaction
items.d: The accusation becomes the thing being done to you. You may feel alone in a sea of accusation. Furious that friends talked, or did not keep something private. Pulled to disappear, to gather your own camp, or to hit back first. Most people feel being asked to account as a rejection and a threat. Expect those pulls in yourself. Slowing down, and seeing that you will not be destroyed, takes real effort.

sources.name: TransformHarm — 9 ways to be accountable when you have been abusive (Everyday Feminism, 2016)
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

items.t: Listening is not agreeing
items.d: You can hear their account without building your reply while they talk. Sit with all of it, not only the parts that do not match your memory. Let what they say add to your picture instead of erasing it. If you notice yourself wanting to defend or attack, stop and listen. Ask how you can understand more, not how you can defend yourself.

sources.name: TransformHarm — suggestions to people called out for abusive behavior (Clamor, 2002)
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)
DanceSafe — power dynamics, accountability and community response

items.t: Being hurt yourself does not answer this
items.d: Survivors can hurt people too. Saying you are a survivor too is not an answer. Neither is saying they have more power than you. It does not settle what you are being asked to face.

sources.name: TransformHarm — 9 ways to be accountable when you have been abusive (Everyday Feminism, 2016)

items.t: The fear is real, and it is not a punishment
items.d: People have lost friends, communities and jobs over this. That lands harder on people who already have less. Losing trust, standing, a role or a place in a scene are possible costs. They come from having caused harm. They are not punishments. Nobody can be made to like or trust you again, even if you change. One of these guides says facing the fear is easier than living in it.

sources.name: TransformHarm — 9 ways to be accountable when you have been abusive (Everyday Feminism, 2016)
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

items.t: It is a process, not one conversation
items.d: Accountability is not confessing and being done. It is practiced over time. Nobody can force it on you or do it for you. It runs on the terms of the person you hurt. It may include things asked of you: a program, some reading, stepping back from events. There is no timeline. It can take months or years, and may never feel finished. One toolkit draws it as a staircase. Stop the harm. See it. Own what it did, without excuses. Repair. Change. Become a healthy part of your community. There is no blueprint, and any step counts. There will be days with little energy. Plan ahead for what helps you recharge.

Mia Mingus — the four parts of accountability
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)
DanceSafe — responding to and repairing a consent violation

items.t: If you share a scene, they lead
items.d: How you handle ending up in the same room is their call, not yours. What they need about contact and shared spaces can change over time. Being different now does not earn you access to them. It does not earn forgiveness. Using the process to push someone toward forgiving you is more of the same harm.

disclosing.title: Telling someone what happened to you
disclosing.intro: If someone hurt you, this is about telling people. Or not. Nothing here says you should. It is about keeping that choice yours, and staying safe once people know.

callout.title: You can think it through with someone first
callout.body: The RAINN hotline is listed under Finding your people. It never asks your name or location. It can help you decide if and when to tell anyone.

groups.title: Whether to tell, and how much

items.t: It is your decision, and only yours
items.d: You can tell one person, many people, or nobody. You never have to. There is no version of this where you owe anyone the story.

sources.name: RAINN: how to tell someone you were sexually assaulted

items.t: You choose how much to say
items.d: A bare minimum is enough. So is the whole story. Being asked a question does not mean you have to answer it. RAINN suggests one line. You wanted them to know it happened. You do not want to share more. Some people push for details anyway. They ask if you are sure, what you were wearing, whether you had been drinking. RAINN tells them not to. If they do it anyway, that is on them. Not on you.

sources.name: RAINN: how to tell someone you were sexually assaulted
RAINN: how to talk with survivors
RAINN: how to help survivors heal

items.t: Waiting is normal, and so is never telling
items.d: Waiting to tell is common. So is never reporting at all. Waiting is not a sign that someone is lying, exaggerating or unsure. Never reporting does not make what happened less real. Fear can keep people quiet long after. Fear of being blamed, rejected or retaliated against. Some tried to tell earlier and were brushed off.

sources.name: RAINN: delayed reporting

items.t: How they react is not yours to manage
items.d: People you tell may get angry, confused, scared, guilty or shocked. Some may doubt you, hint you caused it, or say to get over it. None of that is rooted in the truth. What happened is only ever the fault of the person who did it. If you think they might get angry or violent, pick the place. RAINN advises somewhere public, or with someone you trust present.

sources.name: RAINN: how to tell someone you were sexually assaulted

items.t: Some people are required by law to report
items.d: Teachers, childcare and eldercare workers, medical providers and some religious leaders can be mandatory reporters. If you are under 18 or over 65, they may have to report it. The rules vary by state. That is worth knowing before you choose who to tell.

sources.name: RAINN: how to tell someone you were sexually assaulted

items.t: If the person could find you
items.d: The basics, from RAINN and the National Domestic Violence Hotline: keep your phone charged. Save emergency contacts, under a different name if you need to. Memorize a few numbers. Change your routine and your routes over time. Tell people you trust what is going on. Agree on a code word that means you need help.

sources.name: RAINN: safety planning for survivors of assault, harassment and stalking
National Domestic Violence Hotline: stalking safety planning

items.t: You do not owe them a reply
items.d: Once you have asked them to stop contacting you, that is it. You do not owe a response. Replying tends to tell them their tactics are working. They may offer to stop if you meet in person. That is likely a way to put you at risk. You can block their numbers and accounts. You can change your number or email. Blocking can also prompt them to retaliate or make new accounts. So it is a choice, not a rule. Friends and family can block or report their accounts too.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline: stalking safety planning

items.t: Keeping records is optional
items.d: Saving texts, emails, voicemails and screenshots can help later, if you ever want it. For legal reasons or otherwise. The Hotline suggests noting dates and times. For some people it simply makes what happened feel real. RAINN says to save evidence only if you can do it safely. The Hotline suggests keeping it where the person cannot reach. A separate email account, or a trusted friend.

items.t: Assume your phone and your posts are not private
items.d: A phone or computer can be monitored without you knowing. Browsing history is never fully erased, even in private or incognito mode. For anything sensitive, RAINN and the Hotline both suggest a safer device. A library, a shelter, or a friend's computer. And a new email account the person does not know about. Online, nothing is truly private whatever your settings. Deleted posts can live on as screenshots or server backups. You can ask people not to post about you or tag you. You can turn tagging off.

bystander.title: When it happened to someone you know
bystander.intro: You were not the one hurt, and you did not do it. You are the friend, the crew, the person they told. This is for that. Hotlines are in Communities, under Survivors of abuse and violence.

callout.title: Believe them. You are not the investigator.
callout.body: Believing them is a separate job from deciding what happens to the person named.

groups.title: If someone tells you they were hurt

items.t: Your job is to believe, not to investigate
items.d: Skip the shock, the blame and the why questions. Say you believe them. Say it was not their fault. Do not ask who it was, what they wore, or whether they were drinking. Do not ask how it happened, even out of curiosity. Those questions land as blame.

items.t: Do not push them to report, or to talk
items.d: Not to police, not to a forensic exam, not to say more than they want. Pushing can hurt them all over again. If they do choose to go, offering to go with them is enough.

items.t: Keep it among safe people
items.d: What they told you is not yours to pass on. Do not retell it as gossip. Do not post anything online that could show who they are, or where they go.

items.t: Keep showing up
items.d: Support does not end after one conversation. Check in over time. Offer company, not pressure, and let them set the pace. Once attention turns to the person named, the one hurt tends to get left alone. Make sure it is someone's whole job to keep asking what they want. Do not make them ask for every single thing. Take your own feelings to a friend, a counselor or the hotline, not to them.

groups.title: If the person named is your friend

items.t: Check who you want to believe, and why
items.d: "They seemed so nice" is not evidence. Nice people do terrible things every day. That they were never like that with you proves nothing. Then look at yourself. Do you like one person more? Do you depend on one of them? Do they remind you of someone you like, so you want them to be innocent? Would you lose something by not taking their side? Challenging someone you care about can be a real way of standing by them.

items.t: You can care about them without covering for them
items.d: Being their friend does not mean excusing them or taking their side. It does not mean punishing or humiliating them either. It means helping them see what they did, stop, and take responsibility. Caring about them while supporting the person they hurt is not betrayal. If holding both is too much, take a smaller role or step back. That is allowed.

items.t: Watch for the usual moves, in you and in them
items.d: In you: shielding them from being held to account. Undermining what others are doing. Saying the person hurt was just as responsible. Calling the person hurt crazy. In them: leaving and hoping people forget. Blaming the person they hurt. Blaming whoever raised it. Making the process itself the problem. A friend can name these and stay, rather than join in.

groups.title: If you are the crew, the house or the venue

items.t: Own your part instead of holding a trial
items.d: The person who did the harm is the only one responsible for it. The space still has a part. Name how it contributed, or let it happen. Change what let it happen. Support the person hurt. Support the process of holding the person named to account. Keep the changes going. You do not have to be at the center of it. Offering a room to meet in, or a ride, is a real role. You only need to know enough to keep it safe and private. If it is unfolding at an event right now, tell bar staff or security. They are trained for it.

items.t: Before anyone calls someone out
items.d: A call-out comes from the person hurt's own view of it, and from care. Canceling someone on the spot for a learnable mistake can push them away. Then they are less likely to change. Ask whether a call-in comes first. Ask whether they have done it before, and how much harm was done. Sometimes cutting someone off is what keeps people safe. Revenge, and shaming just to humiliate, are outside the model this section draws on. If your group wants different things, talk it through openly rather than acting alone. If you cannot see past getting even, a different role may fit better. Or stepping back for a while. A public response can also land on the person hurt as gossip, judgment and blame.
