heat.note: Heat illness and water. Three rules if you edit this. (1) The sweating myth is load-bearing: NHS, CDC's traveller page and DanceSafe all say heat stroke means hot dry skin, which describes the heat wave kind, not the dancing kind. NATA's position statement and StatPearls both say exertional heat stroke patients are usually still sweating. If somebody reinstates 'no sweating' here they will teach a reader to rule out the thing that is killing the person in front of them. (2) Ice packs to neck, armpits and groin are near-worthless — 0.028 C/min against the 0.155 that counts as adequate. Most first aid still leads with them. Do not put them back at the top. (3) The fluid ceiling is ~500 mL/h, not the liter this site used to say and most party advice still says; a liter an hour is the whole excretory capacity of a healthy person doing nothing, and MDMA lowers it. See PRIVACY.md rules on denominators — every figure here carries one.
heat.headline: Heat, and water
heat.blurb: How to tell when hot has become dangerous, how to cool somebody down with what is actually in the room, and why drinking too much water swells the brain in people who thought they were being careful.

spot.headline: Telling the difference
spot.lead: Heat exhaustion, drinking too much water and simply being very high on a stimulant share most of their early signs. You are not going to separate them from a symptom list, and neither would a doctor without a blood test. What you are looking for is the one change that decides what you do.

stages.d: Sweating hard, tired, thirsty, a headache starting, cramp in the legs or stomach. They are still making sense. Out of the heat now and it goes no further.
Weak, dizzy, sick, clammy, maybe vomiting, heart going fast. Still lucid — they know where they are and who you are. This is the last rung you can handle yourself.
They stop making sense. Confused, slurring, staggering, unusually aggressive or oddly calm, seizing, or unconscious. This is an ambulance, now.

body: The line between the second rung and the third is not temperature. It is whether they are still thinking straight. Emergency medicine uses the same test: heat stroke is diagnosed on confusion or worse, not on how hot somebody feels to the touch.

Almost every first-aid page you will read says heat stroke means hot, dry skin and no sweating. That describes the kind that happens to an elderly person in a heat wave. The kind that happens to somebody who has been dancing is a different thing, and most people having one are still pouring sweat. If you wait for somebody to stop sweating, you will wait through the entire emergency.
On somebody who has been dancing, an oral thermometer reads about 1 to 3°F low. A forehead or armpit one can be off by 2 to 4°F. So a reading of 101°F fits perfectly well with a core of 104.

emergency.title: Call 911 when they stop making sense
emergency.body: Confusion, slurred speech, staggering, unusual aggression, a seizure, or unconsciousness — in somebody who has been hot, or drinking a lot of water, or both. You do not have to work out which one it is to make the call. It is the same trigger for both. Start cooling while somebody else dials.
emergency.detail: Somebody can seem to come round and then get much worse within minutes. Getting better for a moment is not getting better.

sources.name: NATA position statement — exertional heat illnesses (2015)
StatPearls — heat stroke
Ganio et al., J Athl Train 2009 — validity of non-rectal temperature

cool.headline: Cooling somebody down
cool.lead: With what is in the room. Speed matters more than technique — the harm tracks how long they spend above 104°F, and the target every guideline agrees on is to have them cooled within half an hour of going down.

steps.t: Get them out of the heat
steps.d: Outside, a stairwell, a bathroom, anywhere cooler and away from the crowd. Somebody else calls 911 while you do this. Cooling does not wait for the ambulance to be called, and it does not wait for it to arrive.
As much as the situation allows. Clothing is the insulation you are working against.

steps.t: Cold water on as much skin as you can, and keep it coming
steps.d: A shower, a hose, a bathtub, a sink and a soaked shirt, jugs from behind the bar, ice tipped into water. Not one cold cloth on the forehead — as much surface area as possible, re-wet the moment it stops feeling cold.
steps.note: This is the whole job. Everything else on this list is a detail next to getting a lot of cold water onto a lot of skin.

steps.t: Move air over the wet skin
steps.d: Fan them with a tray, a piece of card, a jacket. Water plus moving air pulls heat out considerably faster than either does alone. Fanning somebody who is dry achieves close to nothing.

steps.t: If you have ice, put it in the right places
steps.d: This is the opposite of what most first aid says, and the measurements are not close. Ice packs on the neck, armpits and groin move core temperature at about a fifth of the rate that counts as good enough. That is barely better than nothing.
steps.note: If somebody hands you cold packs and nothing else, keep soaking and fanning anyway.

steps.t: Keep going 10 to 15 minutes, then hand over
steps.d: You have no way to measure when they have cooled enough, so use the clock instead. Do not stop early because they seem better — that is the point at which people stop, and it is too soon.
steps.note: Cooling somebody too much is not a realistic risk in fifteen minutes with a bucket. Not cooling them enough is the one that happens.

never.title: What not to do
items: Do not give acetaminophen, ibuprofen or aspirin. This is not a fever and they do nothing for it — the body's thermostat is not what has gone wrong. They can make the liver damage and the bleeding problems worse.
Do not hold somebody down. Straining against being held generates heat, and it is one of the reliable ways to make overheating worse in somebody on a stimulant. Clear the space around them instead.
Do not pour drink into somebody who is confused, drowsy or being sick. They can inhale it — and if too much water is the actual problem, you are making it worse.
Do not treat drinking as cooling. Fluids do not bring core temperature down.
Do not delay cooling to take a temperature you cannot take accurately.

sources.name: McDermott et al., J Athl Train 2009 — cooling rates compared
DeMartini et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2015 — 274 consecutive patients, no deaths
BC Emergency Health Services — hyperthermia guideline

water.headline: The other way this goes wrong
water.lead: "Drink water" is the most repeated piece of advice at any event, and the version people act on — drink constantly, drink more if you feel bad — is the version that has put them in intensive care.
body: Your kidneys can only get rid of so much water: somewhere around a liter an hour at the absolute best, in a healthy person with nothing else going on. Stimulants and MDMA stop your body clearing it properly. Drink past what you can pass and the sodium in your blood dilutes, cells swell, and the cells with nowhere to swell into are the ones in your skull.

In four pooled trials, 96 healthy adults were given an ordinary dose of MDMA in a lab — sitting still, air conditioned, drinking as much or as little as they wanted. Among those left to drink freely, 37% became hyponatremic. Among the 15 whose fluids were limited, none did. Nobody in that study was dancing, and nobody was in a hot room.

items.t: What it looks like
items.d: Three signs belong to this one and not to heat. They look puffy, especially the fingers and face, and rings or shoes feel tight. They have gained weight, not lost it, after hours of effort. And they have not peed in a long time, even though they keep drinking.
items.note: The most useful thing you have is not a sign, it is the story. If somebody has been drinking water for hours, say that to the medics out loud. It is what makes a clinician check their sodium instead of treating them for something else.

items.t: What to do
items.d: Stop the fluids. All of them, including sports drinks. If they are fully awake and not vomiting, salty food is the right thing — salt without water is exactly what they need. Sit them somewhere cool and stay with them.

items.t: It can arrive hours later
items.d: Symptoms can start within 24 hours of leaving, in somebody who seemed fine on the way out. Do not let them go home alone to sleep it off. Tell them, and tell whoever they are with, what to watch for.

emergency.title: This one is also 911
emergency.body: A seizure, confusion or drowsiness, vomiting with a bad headache, trouble breathing, or frothy spit. It is the same trigger as heat stroke — they stop making sense. The difference is what you do next: cool them, but do not give them anything to drink.

water.note: Being honest about the size of this: more accidents at events come from overheating than from over-drinking, by a wide margin. What makes water intoxication worth its own section is that it turns into a 911 emergency in people who believed they were doing the careful thing.

sources.name: Hew-Butler et al. — 3rd International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus (2015)
Atila et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024 — MDMA and hyponatremia, 4 pooled trials
Rosenson et al., J Emerg Med 2007 — MDMA hyponatremia case series

items.t: Two to three cups an hour, not four
items.d: A liter an hour is everything a healthy person's kidneys can clear while doing nothing at all. It was never a safety ceiling. It was an estimate of how much a dancer sweats. And MDMA lowers what you can clear.
items.note: People have become seriously ill at intakes as low as about two cups an hour. There is no volume that is guaranteed safe; there is only less risk.

items.t: Thirst is a better guide than a schedule
items.d: The advice to get ahead of it came from workplaces and endurance sport. In dance settings it is the exact instruction that has put people in hospital. In the case reports, “stay ahead of thirst” keeps coming back from the people who followed it.

sources.name: Hew-Butler et al. — EAH consensus, drinking behavior

items.t: Electrolyte drinks do less than they sound like they do
items.d: Every sports drink is more dilute than your blood, so it still adds free water faster than it adds salt. Better than the same volume of plain water, but it does not buy permission to drink more, and it will not prevent this. Volume is what hurts you. Salty food is the thing that moves sodium without adding more water to clear.

items.t: Get off the floor before you need to
items.d: In a study that measured real clubs — 29°C and 90% humidity among the dancers — an hour of dancing raised core temperature by 1.8°C, and four hours without a break modeled out to 39.1°C. Twenty minutes somewhere cooler, before anything is wrong, does more for you than anything you can drink.

sources.name: McNeill & Parsons — Heat stress in night-clubs (1996)

risk.headline: Who it hits hardest

items.t: The first few days in it
items.d: This is the best-evidenced item on the page and the one nobody mentions. Your body adapts to heat over about one to two weeks, and it loses that adaptation within days of not being in it. OSHA's figures on heat deaths at work: more than 70% happen in somebody's first week, and close to half on their first day, or their first day back after time away.
items.note: It is not about being fit or being used to hard work. It is about how recently your body was last doing this in this heat.

sources.name: OSHA — protecting new and returning workers
Daanen et al., Sports Med 2018 — how fast heat acclimatization decays

items.t: Not being able to go somewhere cooler
items.d: The single largest risk factor is having nowhere to get out of it. Across Las Vegas and Los Angeles, researchers estimated that half of all deaths among people experiencing homelessness in Clark County were attributable to temperature — a figure they described as orders of magnitude above the general population. In Maricopa County, Arizona, 208 of the 430 heat deaths recorded in 2025 were among people who were unhoused.
items.note: Of the indoor heat deaths in that county, 94% happened in homes that had air conditioning. In 72% of those, it was not running — broken, or shut off because of the bill.

sources.name: Lin et al., Am J Epidemiol 2024 — temperature-attributable mortality among people experiencing homelessness
Maricopa County — heat-associated deaths report, 2025

items.t: Using drugs in a heat wave
items.d: Of the 430 heat deaths in Maricopa County in 2025, 236 involved substances, and 194 of those involved a stimulant. That is a count of who died, not a rate — it cannot tell you how much more likely it is. The one study that measured the risk properly, across the 2021 heat dome in British Columbia, found substance use disorder raised the odds of dying by about a quarter. Real, but smaller than you might expect, and much smaller than being poor, which roughly doubled them.
items.note: Stimulants raise the heat your body makes and how long you stay in it. Both matter more in a heat wave than on a dancefloor, because a heat wave lasts days.

sources.name: McLean et al., Environ Res Health 2024 — deaths in the 2021 BC heat dome

items.t: Medication, with a caveat about how sure anyone is
items.d: The standard warning list is longer than the evidence for it. When researchers pooled 35 heat-stress experiments, only strong anticholinergics and non-selective beta blockers actually raised core temperature; antidepressants, antihistamines and antipsychotics did not. The real-world data disagrees with the lab. Among older adults, heat waves plus antipsychotics, loop diuretics or anticholinergics meant clearly more heat hospitalizations. During the BC heat dome, people with schizophrenia taking antipsychotics had roughly 2.4 times the odds of an accident.
items.note: The one with a warning printed on the label is topiramate, sold as Topamax and used for seizures and migraine: it can reduce sweating, most often in children. Do not stop a prescribed medication over this. Take the heat more seriously instead.

sources.name: Hospers et al., eClinicalMedicine 2024 — meta-analysis of 35 heat-stress trials
Layton et al., PLoS One 2020 — medications and heat hospitalization in 9,721 people
Chen et al., Sci Rep 2025 — antipsychotics and death in the BC heat dome
FDA label — topiramate, decreased sweating

items.t: Alcohol, and what is actually wrong with it
items.d: Not what you have been told. A review of eight studies found alcohol did not reduce sweating and did not raise core temperature — the dehydration only showed up at the highest doses tested. The link between drinking and dying in heat waves is real and well documented; what has never been studied is the obvious explanation, which is that drinking changes whether you notice you are in trouble and whether you do anything about it.
items.note: Worth saying plainly: this is a gap in the research, not a finding. Treat alcohol in heat as a reason to have somebody watching out for you rather than as something that dries you out.

sources.name: Morris et al., Environ Health 2024 — alcohol and thermoregulation, scoping review

items.t: Smaller bodies have less room for error
items.d: Less total body water means a given surplus moves your sodium further. In the MDMA case reports the skew is stark — in one poison-center series of 73 people with hyponatremia, 55 were women, and women had about four times the odds of it. Some of that is body size and some is how much people drink, but it is not nothing.
items.note: This is not a reason for anyone else to relax. It means the margin is narrower if you are small, not that it is wide if you are not.

sources.name: Rosenson et al., J Emerg Med 2007

items.t: Hours, not doses
items.d: In 488 runners tested at the end of a marathon, 13% were hyponatremic. The things that predicted it were gaining weight during the race and being out there more than four hours — not sex, and not what they drank. Time spent in it is the exposure.

sources.name: Almond et al., N Engl J Med 2005 — hyponatremia among marathon runners

risk.lead: Two of the things on this list are much better established than the advice you will have heard, and two are much weaker. Both are worth knowing, because acting on the weak ones instead of the strong ones is how people get caught out.

market.note: HAND-WRITTEN. Explains the MECHANICS of an unregulated supply — why potency varies, why adulterants appear, why the same source is not the same product. Deliberately contains NOTHING that helps anyone buy: no marketplaces, no vendor guidance, no sourcing, no advice on avoiding detection while purchasing. That line is the difference between harm reduction and a buying guide.
market.headline: Why the supply is like this

blocks.title: Enforcement pushes drugs toward stronger, smaller forms
blocks.body: This has a name: the Iron Law of Prohibition. When a supply is squeezed, the economics favor whatever is most compact — a trafficker faces roughly the same penalty for a small package as a large one, so potency per unit of volume goes up. That is the path the US market has taken: prescription pills to heroin, heroin to fentanyl, and now fentanyl to nitazenes. Each step is smaller, stronger, and harder to dose.
blocks.sotu: It also explains why cracking down on one drug so reliably produces a stronger replacement, rather than less supply.

sources.name: Beletsky & Davis — Prohibition’s Iron Law, revisited (Int J Drug Policy, 2017)

blocks.title: Potency is an accident of mixing, not a recipe
blocks.body: Fentanyl is active in microgram amounts. Mixing micrograms evenly through a kilogram of powder is an industrial process, and this is not an industrial process. What reaches you was cut and re-cut by people without equipment to do it evenly, so two bags off the same batch can differ, and so can two ends of the same bag.
blocks.sotu: This is the whole reason “start with much less than usual” is the first rule, and why testing a dissolved portion of everything beats testing a pinch.

sources.name: NIDA — Fentanyl

blocks.title: Adulterants are added for reasons that have nothing to do with you
blocks.body: Xylazine lengthens a short fentanyl high, which makes a supply feel more like heroin and reduces how often someone needs to buy. Levamisole and lidocaine bulk out cocaine and mimic its numbing. Caffeine and diphenhydramine are cheap filler. None of these are chosen for effect on the person taking them — they are chosen for cost, weight, and how the product behaves in a market.
blocks.sotu: Which is why the adulterant in your supply can change without anything about your source changing.

sources.name: DEA — Fentanyl

blocks.title: A trusted source is not a quality control system
blocks.body: The person selling to you is usually near the end of a long chain and did not make what they are selling. They can be completely honest with you and still not know what is in it — most people at that end of the chain are using the same supply themselves. Trust tells you about a person. It tells you nothing about a batch.
blocks.sotu: This is the single most common way people are caught out: the supply changed, the source did not.

blocks.title: Ratings and “lab tested” claims are not verification
blocks.body: Buying through a screen adds review scores, vendor histories and sometimes a photographed lab report — the visual furniture of a regulated market. None of it is verification. A rating measures whether previous orders arrived and matched a description, which is a delivery record, not a chemical one. A lab report can be real and still describe a different batch than the one in your hand, or belong to someone else entirely, or be edited.
blocks.sotu: Every earlier point on this page still applies: the person selling is rarely the person who made it, potency still varies within a batch, and nobody in the chain tested what you received.

blocks.title: Counterfeit pills are the sharpest version of this
blocks.body: A pressed pill looks finished and identical to the next one, which is exactly what makes it dangerous — it carries the visual signals of a regulated product with none of the process behind them. Pill presses do not distribute a microgram-scale drug evenly, so within a single batch one pill can hold a survivable amount and the next several times that.
blocks.sotu: An imprint, a color, and a shape can all be copied. None of them are evidence of what is inside.

sources.name: DEA — Fentanyl

blocks.title: Distance does not change the chemistry
blocks.body: It is easy to believe a supply that arrives in the mail is cleaner than one bought in person — better presented, more anonymous, further from anyone you might blame. The adulterants that matter get added early, near production, long before anything is packaged or listed. Where the last handover happened does not change what is in the powder.
blocks.sotu: Which is why a sample you did not test yourself is an unknown regardless of how it reached you.

close.title: What all of this adds up to
close.body: None of it is a reason to give up, and none of it makes anything safe. But it does point at four things that genuinely lower your odds: assume a new batch is stronger than the last one, test what you can, start with much less than you mean to take, and don't be alone. Nobody is handing those down as rules — they are just what everything above works out to in practice.

scope.title: What you won't find here
scope.body: Where to buy, who to buy from, and how not to get caught. Not because anyone here is squeamish about it, but because none of it would keep you safer. Every risk on this page comes from what is in the drugs, and where you got them does not change what is in them. Testing, dose, and not being alone do.

name-warnings.note: Street names that MISLEAD - the name says one drug, the market sells another. Renders as a warning on the substance page and the names become searchable aliases. Every entry needs a live-verified source; this file exists because a name can be the adulteration vector.

2c-b.text: “Tusi” and “pink cocaine” sound like this substance — they almost never are it. Of 960 pink powders DEA seized since 2020, only 4 contained any 2C-B. The pink powder sold under these names is typically a ketamine mix, often with MDMA or caffeine, and sometimes opioids. It also usually contains no cocaine. If it is pink powder, treat it as an unknown ketamine blend, not as 2C-B.

calling.headline: If you call 911, what happens to you?
calling.lead: This is the question that stops people, and it deserves a real answer rather than reassurance.
body: Fear of police is the most commonly documented reason people don't call for help during an overdose. That fear is not irrational, and telling you it is would be dishonest.

Every state, plus DC, now has a Good Samaritan overdose law. New Mexico was first in 2007; Kansas and Wyoming were the last, in 2024 and 2025. But what those laws actually protect varies enormously, and the gaps are the part nobody tells you.

limits.headline: What these laws generally do not cover

items.t: Being arrested
items.d: Only 25 states and DC explicitly protect against arrest or being taken into custody. In roughly half the country the law protects you from being prosecuted, and says nothing about being handcuffed first.

items.t: Anything beyond possession
items.d: Protection is generally limited to low-level possession and paraphernalia. 39 states and DC expressly include paraphernalia. Selling, sharing, or handing someone drugs is usually excluded outright.

items.t: A homicide charge
items.d: 35 states plus DC have a drug-induced homicide law, and Good Samaritan protection reaches that charge in only three: Kentucky, Vermont, and Virginia. Someone who used alongside a person who died has been charged with homicide after calling for help. In most states the Good Samaritan law does not stop that.

items.t: An outstanding warrant
items.d: Not protected. In 12 states and DC, acting in good faith expressly excludes seeking help while a warrant is being executed.

items.t: Probation or parole
items.d: Only 27 states and DC extend protection to a violation. 23 states do not.

items.t: Evidence of other crimes
items.d: 31 states and DC specify that immunity is not grounds for suppressing evidence of something else found at the scene.

variations.headline: Where your state changes the answer entirely

items.t: Texas and Utah
items.d: An affirmative defense, not immunity. That means it is raised at trial, after you have been charged — not a reason you don't get charged.

items.t: Alabama, Indiana, Maine, Oklahoma, Wisconsin
items.d: The caller is protected. The person who overdosed is not. Louisiana is the reverse.

items.t: Alabama, Iowa, North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas
items.d: Only the first person to call is covered.

items.t: Indiana
items.d: The only state that requires the caller to administer naloxone.

variations.note: Most laws also require you to call in good faith, stay on the scene, and cooperate with responders. Leaving can cost you the protection.

calling.bottom: None of this is a reason not to call. It is the reason to know what your state actually does before you are standing over someone. Look it up before you need it, not while you need it.

sources.name: LAPPA — Good Samaritan Fatal Overdose Prevention and Drug-Induced Homicide: Summary of State Laws (research current July 2025)
GAO-21-248 — Most States Have Good Samaritan Laws (2021)

law.headline: Where the law actually stands
law.blurb: Dated, because all of this moves. Anything here without a date should be treated as unverified.

items.t: Fentanyl test strips are legal almost everywhere — but not quite
items.d: As of July 1 2026, possessing drug-checking equipment is outside paraphernalia law in 47 states, DC and 4 territories. Three states still potentially reach it: Iowa, North Dakota, Texas. Strips for xylazine are narrower — 11 more states wrote their carve-out for fentanyl only, so it does not cover xylazine there. Florida and Wisconsin cover fentanyl and xylazine but not medetomidine or nitazene strips.

sources.name: LAPPA — Drug Checking Equipment fact sheet, July 2026

items.t: Federal money stopped paying for test strips in April 2026
items.d: HHS guidance dated April 24 2026 bars federal funding from buying or distributing syringes, safer smoking supplies, sterile water, and test strips of any kind — including fentanyl, xylazine and medetomidine. Test strips were explicitly fundable as recently as July 2025. Naloxone, wound care, sharps disposal, condoms and HIV/HCV testing are still funded. Legal to own is not the same as available near you, and this is why the two can diverge.

sources.name: SAMHSA — Dear Colleague letter, April 24 2026

items.t: Xylazine and medetomidine are not federally scheduled
items.d: Neither is a controlled substance as of August 2026. Both are veterinary sedatives. Nine states have scheduled xylazine on their own. Medetomidine reports to federal forensic labs went from 12 in 2021 to 8,391 in 2025.

sources.name: DEA Diversion Control — Xylazine fact sheet, May 2026
DEA Diversion Control — Medetomidine fact sheet, March 2026

items.t: Fentanyl-related substances are permanently Schedule I as a class
items.d: The HALT Fentanyl Act became law on July 16 2025. It controls fentanyl-like compounds by chemical structure rather than one at a time, and extends the same mandatory minimums — 400 grams for ten years, 40 grams for five. Supporters say it stops traffickers from changing one molecule to stay legal. Critics, including civil rights and drug policy organizations, say it schedules substances without individual evidence of harm and sweeps in compounds that may be inert. The Sentencing Commission added a rebuttable exception, effective November 1 2026, for substances shown to be significantly less potent than fentanyl or to counteract it.

sources.name: Public Law 119-26 (HALT Fentanyl Act), enacted July 16 2025

items.t: Cannabis rescheduling is half-done, and the main question is undecided
items.d: A final rule effective April 28 2026 moved cannabis to Schedule III only where it is in an FDA-approved drug product or under a state medical license. Everything else, including all adult-use cannabis, stays Schedule I. A separate hearing on whether cannabis generally should move concluded July 15 2026; briefs were not due until August 17 2026 and no decision has issued. Three petitions challenging the rule are pending in the D.C. Circuit. Anyone telling you the outcome right now is guessing.

sources.name: Federal Register — final rule, 91 FR 22714, effective April 28 2026

items.t: Syringe programs: federal funds still cannot buy the syringes
items.d: A rider carried in every appropriations act, including the one enacted February 3 2026, bars federal money from buying needles or syringes anywhere. Federal funds can support the rest of a program — staff, testing, naloxone, referrals — but only where a health department has made a determination of need with CDC. 37 states, DC and Puerto Rico authorize syringe programs; roughly 587 were operating as of June 2026. Five states have none at all: Kansas, Mississippi, Nebraska, South Dakota, Wyoming.

sources.name: Public Law 119-75, Sec. 525, enacted February 3 2026
LAPPA — Syringe Services Programs, July 2026

items.t: Overdose prevention centers: two operating, contested federally
items.d: Two sanctioned programs operate in the US — OnPoint NYC's two locations in Manhattan, and one in Providence run by Project Weber/RENEW, which Rhode Island authorized by statute and extended to March 1 2028. Vermont has authorized one that has not opened. Federal law, 21 U.S.C. 856, makes maintaining a place for drug use an offense, and an executive order signed July 24 2025 directs review of federally funded organizations operating such sites. No prosecution of an operating site is documented. The pressure so far has been money: OnPoint reported losing over $2 million in federal grants.

sources.name: Rhode Island Department of Health — harm reduction centers

items.t: Overdose deaths have fallen four years running — but not everywhere
items.d: CDC's provisional counts show 67,798 deaths in the 12 months ending March 2026, down 12.3% year over year and below the 2019 figure, from a peak of 110,393 in 2022. Seven jurisdictions rose over that period rather than fell, led by New Mexico at +28.3%, Colorado at +11.6% and Arizona at +5.3%. A national decline is not your county's decline.

sources.name: CDC/NCHS — Provisional Drug Overdose Death Counts (data updated August 12 2026)

money.headline: Follow the money
money.blurb: Where the funding actually comes from, and why that decides what exists near you.
body: Roughly $58.6 billion in opioid settlement money is being paid to state and local governments over 18 years, with payments having started in 2022. Settlement agreements generally require 85% to go to opioid remediation.

How it is being spent is documented and uneven. About $6 billion was distributed through 2023. Of the roughly $2.2 billion of that which jurisdictions actually reported spending, syringe services received 1.7% — about $37.3 million — while 41.3% went to an “other” bucket that mixes law enforcement with treatment workforce and multi-category spending. These are 2022–23 expenditures released in December 2024, and the database itself is described as incomplete. Roughly a third was appropriated, a third held in reserve, and a third is unaccounted for because some jurisdictions have not reported at all.
Of twelve states that committed in writing to disclose every dollar, seven had kept that commitment by late 2024. Four jurisdictions — Alaska, DC, Louisiana and Mississippi — had published nothing.

This is the most direct lever most people have. Settlement spending is decided by state and county officials, in public processes, and it is now the main legal channel for the supplies federal money stopped covering in April 2026.

LAPPA — Opioid Litigation Proceeds, March 2025

voice.headline: Making yourself heard, in a way that counts
voice.blurb: Congressional staff were surveyed on what actually moves them. The answers are not what most advocacy pages tell you.

what.headline: What has influence, when a position isn't already fixed

items.d: An in-person visit from a constituent
An email you wrote yourself
A letter you wrote yourself
A phone call — which outranks a visit from a paid lobbyist, at 83%
A form email someone else wrote for you

what.note: A prewritten template scores 36 points below the same message in your own words. That is why this page will never hand you one to send.

gap.headline: The two things that work, that almost nobody includes

items.t: What it means for your district
items.d: 91% of staff call this helpful. 9% of constituents include it. Name your county, the program that closed, the wait for a treatment bed where you live.

items.t: Your own story
items.d: 79% of staff call this helpful. 18% of constituents include it. You do not owe anyone this, and you should weigh what it costs you to put it in writing to a government office. But it is the single most under-used thing.

gap.note: Include both and your message is in rare company. Also say plainly what you want them to do — a specific ask, named bill if you have one.

who.headline: Reaching the right office
body: Contact your own representatives. Offices are guided to prioritize their own constituents and may refer everyone else back to their own member, so a message to a senator two states away is generally set aside.
District and state offices matter as much as Washington. Staff rate district office hours and local events among the strongest signals of what people at home think.
The Capitol switchboard will connect you to any House or Senate office: (202) 224-3121.
who.privacy: These are outside links. Following one leaves this app, and the site you land on will see your visit the way any website does. Nightlight never asks where you are and never looks anything up on your behalf.

giving.headline: Before you give
body: A 501(c)(3) donation is tax-deductible. A 501(c)(4) is not, because it can lobby without limit — Drug Policy Action and the Marijuana Policy Project are the (c)(4) arms of groups listed above.

Charity Navigator only rates US 501(c)(3) organizations with three years of filed returns, which excludes most small, new, and drug-user-led groups. An unrated organization is not a bad one, and the groups closest to this work are the ones most likely to be missing.

practice.note: HAND-WRITTEN. Practice exercises, not a quiz. There is no score, no timer, no streak and no fail state anywhere in this file, and adding one would break the thing it is for. Content mirrors the real guidance in site/js/views/help.js and data/testing.json — if those change, this must change with them.
practice.intro: Reading how to do something and being able to do it at 3am are different. These let you practice, with nothing riding on it.

strip.title: Read the strip
strip.why: One line means positive. That is backwards from every other test people have used, and it is the single most misread result in drug checking. Worth getting wrong here, where it costs nothing.

cards.alt: A test strip showing one line, in the control area only.
cards.right: One line is POSITIVE — fentanyl is in the sample.
cards.explain: The strip works by competition: fentanyl in the sample blocks the test line from forming. The drug being present makes a line disappear. That is why it reads backwards from a pregnancy test.

cards.alt: A test strip showing two lines.
cards.right: Two lines is NEGATIVE — nothing detected in what you tested.
cards.explain: A second line can be very faint and still count as negative. Wait the full time your instructions give before deciding — a faint line can appear and then fade. And a negative is about the sample you dissolved, not the rest of the bag.

cards.alt: A test strip showing no lines at all.
cards.right: No lines means the test failed — it tells you nothing.
cards.explain: No lines, or a line only on the end you dipped, means the strip did not run properly. Too much liquid, too little, or a bad strip. Use a new one; do not read it as negative.

overdose.title: Walk through an overdose
overdose.why: The order matters more than people expect, and it changed recently. Nothing here is timed and nothing is scored — take as long as you want on each one.

steps.scene: Someone is slumped over and not moving. You are the only person there.

options.label: Look at their chest for breathing
Shake them and shout their name

steps.right: Breathing first. Look at their chest.
steps.explain: This changed in 2025. Sedatives now common in the supply — xylazine, medetomidine — can leave someone impossible to wake while their breathing is fine. Checking whether they respond first can mislead you in both directions. Bad breathing or no response, either one, means act.

onWrong.shake: Reasonable, and it used to be step one. But someone can be unwakeable and breathing fine on a sedative — the chest tells you more than the shoulder does.
onWrong.call: You will call, and soon. But look at their chest first so you can tell the dispatcher whether they are breathing, which is the thing that changes what happens next.
onWrong.naloxone: Not wrong, and if it is already in your hand it costs seconds. But look at the chest first — you need to know what you are treating and whether it is working.

steps.scene: Their breathing is slow and sounds like snoring. They do not wake when you shout or rub their breastbone.

options.label: Wait a few minutes to see if they come to
Try to walk them around or give them a cold shower
Put them to bed on their side and check later

steps.explain: Snoring or gurgling breathing is an obstructed airway, not sleep. If you are alone and naloxone is in your hand, give it first, then call — with two people, one calls while the other doses.

onWrong.wait: Waiting is the thing that does the damage here. Lack of oxygen is what causes it, and it is happening while you wait.
onWrong.coffee: These do not work and they waste the minutes that do. Cold water and walking cannot make someone breathe.
onWrong.sleep: Leaving someone in this state is how the airway closes the rest of the way and the breathing stops, with nobody in the room. Snoring here is the airway, not sleep.

steps.scene: You gave one dose of naloxone. Two minutes later their breathing is better but they are still asleep and confused.

options.label: It worked — watch them and stay
It failed — give more doses until they wake up
They are stable now, so you can head off

steps.right: It worked. Breathing is the measure, not waking.
steps.explain: Judge by their chest, not their eyes. Someone can stay asleep after a reversal that already worked — that is the sedative, not a failed dose. Naloxone wears off in 30–90 minutes and most opioids last longer, so they can go under again.

onWrong.more: Understandable, but stacking doses to force someone awake can throw them into hard withdrawal for no gain. If breathing improved, it worked.
onWrong.leave: This is the most common mistake that turns a successful reversal into an accident. Naloxone wears off before the drug does, and if you have gone, no one is there when their breathing drops again.

steps.scene: A different night. You gave naloxone, breathing improved, but they are still deeply sedated — and you know tranq is around.
steps.ask: What does naloxone do about the xylazine?

options.label: Nothing — but you still give it
Skip naloxone if you think it is xylazine

steps.right: Nothing for the xylazine — and you give it anyway.
steps.explain: Xylazine and medetomidine are not opioids, so naloxone cannot lift their sedation. It still reverses the fentanyl that is almost always with them, and the fentanyl is what stops breathing. Watch their breathing rather than whether they wake up.

onWrong.reverses: It does not — they are alpha-2 agonists, a different receptor entirely. That is why someone stays sedated after a reversal that worked.
onWrong.skip: This is the dangerous version of knowing about xylazine. Skipping naloxone leaves the fentanyl unreversed, and the fentanyl is the part that stops breathing.

close.title: That is the whole protocol
close.body: Breathing first. Naloxone even when unsure. Judge by the chest. Stay. If you want the full version with sources, it is on the Emergency tab — and a real course with a certificate, often with free naloxone at the end, is one tap away below.

regional.headline: There is no single American drug supply. There are at least four.
regional.summary: Of 90 drugs detected routinely in mail-in drug checking, only 20 turn up everywhere at similar rates. The other 70 are concentrated — some 80 to 90 percent confined to a single region. A drug is counted as regional when one region accounts for at least 35% of the times it is detected nationally.
regional.caveat: This is not a random sample of the US drug supply. It is what reaches harm reduction programs and drug-checking partners, and that coverage is uneven — strong in some states, thin in others.

substances.desc: A fentanyl synthesis precursor that signals clandestine manufacturing activity.

substances.desc: Benadryl, a sedating antihistamine added to opioids to enhance sedation and to compensate for shorter-acting opioids.

substances.desc: An industrial precursor compound related to certain fentanyl synthesis routes.

substances.desc: A basic industrial chemical used as a starting material in fentanyl precursor synthesis.

substances.desc: A metabolite and synthesis byproduct of cocaine that signals less-refined product or aggressive cutting practices.

substances.name: phenacetin
substances.desc: A discontinued analgesic widely used as a cocaine cutting agent because its appearance and properties mimic powder cocaine.

substances.desc: A local anesthetic added to cocaine to mimic the numbing effect of pure cocaine when tasted.

substances.desc: A synthesis-related compound that appears as a manufacturing impurity.

substances.desc: A synthesis byproduct that appears in less-refined cocaine.

substances.desc: Generic sugars (lactose, sucrose, glucose) used as inexpensive cuts in powder drug supplies.

substances.desc: A natural alkaloid from the coca plant that appears in less-refined cocaine product.

substances.desc: A synthetic cathinone ('bath salt') with stimulant effects, recently emerging as an adulterant in MDMA and other supplies.

substances.desc: A glycerin derivative used industrially as a humectant and solvent; appears in some drug supplies as a cut or carrier.

substances.desc: A novel nitazene-family synthetic opioid that has appeared in the supply as an emerging fentanyl alternative.

substances.desc: A precursor specific to p-fluorofentanyl manufacture, indicating that synthesis route.

substances.name: tetracaine
substances.desc: A potent local anesthetic used as a cocaine bulking agent, producing the numbing sensation associated with cocaine quality.

substances.desc: Another veterinary alpha-2 sedative now appearing in the fentanyl supply, with effects similar to xylazine and not reversed by naloxone.

substances.name: 2C-B
substances.desc: A phenethylamine psychedelic with stimulant and visual properties, popular in some recreational scenes.

substances.name: methyl ecgonidine (MED)
substances.desc: A cocaine pyrolysis product that forms when cocaine is smoked, also a marker of less-refined product.

substances.name: NPP
substances.desc: N-phenethyl-4-piperidone, the most common direct precursor used in clandestine fentanyl manufacture.

substances.name: quinine
substances.desc: A bitter alkaloid traditionally used as a heroin cutting agent to mimic heroin's bitter taste.

substances.name: benzyl benzoate
substances.desc: A solvent and plasticizer that can appear as a carrier or contaminant.

substances.name: niacinamide
substances.desc: Vitamin B3, used as a cheap inert bulking agent in powder drug supplies.

substances.name: dimethyl sulfone (methylsulfonylmethane MSM)
substances.desc: An over-the-counter supplement sold as a joint-health product, used as a methamphetamine cutting agent.

substances.name: benzoylecgonine (BZ)
substances.desc: The main human metabolite of cocaine, sometimes detected in samples as a marker of product handling or contamination.

substances.name: nicotine
substances.desc: Trace nicotine contamination can come from handling or paraphernalia; rarely a deliberate additive.

substances.desc: Klonopin, a long-acting prescription benzodiazepine; combination with opioids substantially increases overdose risk.

substances.desc: A novel synthetic compound detected in recent supply samples whose pharmacology is poorly characterized.

substances.name: ortho-methylfentanyl
substances.desc: A fentanyl analog with high potency; its detection signals diversified or older-route synthesis.

substances.name: meconin
substances.desc: A minor alkaloid of opium present as a heroin manufacturing residue.

substances.name: erythritol
substances.desc: A sugar alcohol sweetener used as a bulking agent, especially in fentanyl supplies.

substances.name: phenethylbromide
substances.desc: An alkylating reagent used in fentanyl-class synthesis.

substances.name: benzyl alcohol
substances.desc: A preservative solvent occasionally used as a carrier in injection drug preparations.

substances.name: 1-phenethyl-4-hydroxypiperidine
substances.desc: A fentanyl precursor / synthesis intermediate detected as a manufacturing byproduct.

substances.name: acetanilide
substances.desc: A precursor and synthesis impurity, originally a historical fever medication.

substances.name: caffeine
substances.desc: A stimulant used as a bulking agent in MDMA, cocaine, and other stimulants to mimic perceived strength.

substances.name: benzocaine
substances.desc: A local anesthetic commonly added to cocaine and to powders sold as cocaine to fake the numbing test.

substances.name: dextromethorphan
substances.desc: An over-the-counter cough suppressant with dissociative effects at high doses; sometimes added to drug supplies.

substances.name: carfentanil
substances.desc: An extremely potent fentanyl analog (roughly 100 times stronger than fentanyl itself) originally developed as an elephant tranquilizer.

substances.name: tetramethyl-4-AP
substances.desc: A piperidine derivative whose pharmacology in the supply context is not well characterized.

substances.name: N,N-Dimethylamphetamine (DMA)
substances.desc: An amphetamine-class compound that appears as a methamphetamine impurity or as a distinct emerging substance.

substances.name: 1-propionyl-4-anilinopiperidine
substances.desc: A fentanyl-class synthesis intermediate that appears as a manufacturing impurity.

substances.desc: A synthesis precursor specific to ortho-methylfentanyl manufacture.

substances.desc: A fentanyl-related synthesis intermediate.

substances.desc: A veterinary deworming agent added to most cocaine in North America; chronic exposure can cause serious immune system damage and skin necrosis.

substances.desc: A novel fentanyl-related compound whose pharmacology is poorly characterized.

substances.name: noscapine
substances.desc: A non-narcotic opium alkaloid that appears in heroin as a residue from opium poppy processing.

substances.name: xylazine
substances.desc: A veterinary sedative ('tranq') increasingly mixed into fentanyl; not reversed by naloxone, prolongs sedation, and causes severe skin wounds with chronic use.

substances.name: 4-anilinopiperidine
substances.desc: A core fentanyl precursor whose international trafficking has been increasingly restricted.

substances.name: melatonin
substances.desc: A sleep-cycle hormone available over the counter; rarely a deliberate drug additive, more often packaging or co-use signal.

substances.name: N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT)

rx.intro: If you take prescribed medication and also use other drugs, the prescription changes the math. None of this is a reason to stop a medication - stopping methadone or bupe abruptly is its own danger. It is a reason to know which combinations carry documented risk.

items.with: Benzos, alcohol, other opioids, any depressant
items.claim: Boxed warning: profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death. This is the label's strongest warning, not fine print.

sources.name: Methadose label (DailyMed)

items.with: Using benzos while on methadone treatment
items.claim: Federal guidance says treatment should not be withheld or stopped over benzodiazepine use - it should be managed. If a program threatens to cut you off, that is not what the guidance says.

sources.name: SAMHSA TIP 63

items.claim: Methadone carries a boxed warning for life-threatening heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation); the risk adds up with other drugs that do the same.

sources.name: Methadose label (DailyMed)

items.claim: Boosters can change methadone levels - worth a per-pair check.

sources.name: Norvir label
Liverpool interaction checker

items.claim: Label warning: serious risk including death, especially with injection or misuse. Same rule as methadone: this is managed, not a reason to lose treatment.

sources.name: Suboxone label (DailyMed)
SAMHSA TIP 63

items.claim: Precipitated withdrawal risk is real and highest within 24-48 hours of fentanyl use - in one study of 1,679 people, 22% had severe withdrawal starting under 24 hours. This is observational evidence, not a trial.

sources.name: Study (PubMed 34816821)

items.with: Using fentanyl or heroin on top of bupe
items.claim: Higher bupe doses blunt other opioids' effects. That is pharmacology, not protection - it is not overdose-proof.

sources.name: SAMHSA TIP 63

items.with: Opioids after a missed dose or stopping
items.claim: The label warns of heightened overdose vulnerability: tolerance drops during treatment, and trying to push through the blockade with a large amount is what stops breathing.

sources.name: Vivitrol label (DailyMed)

items.claim: Labels list amphetamines among drugs with serotonin syndrome risk. Separately, a controlled human study found SSRIs blunt most of MDMA's effect - which people sometimes chase with more. Neither fact makes the mix predictable.

sources.name: Zoloft label (class labeling)

items.claim: Contraindicated on every label, with documented severe reactions - this is the serotonergic combination with the worst record.

sources.name: Case report (PubMed 2884326)

items.claim: Tramadol's label carries both a serotonin syndrome warning and a seizure warning, and both risks rise when combined with SSRIs/SNRIs.

items.claim: Documented deaths and near-deaths with ritonavir - one MDMA fatality showed roughly ten times the expected blood level. Case reports, not rates; the mechanism is strong.

sex.note: Hand-curated. Written for people who are going to be out, using, and having sex, because that is what happens. Nothing here is conditional on stopping any of it.
sex.headline: Sexual health
sex.blurb: Barriers, PrEP and PEP, emergency contraception, the drug interactions that actually put people in the hospital, and an honest answer about drink testing.

framing.headline: Why this page is not a list of precautions
body: The usual nightlife advice — watch your drink, don't go out alone, don't wear that — has a measured effect, and it is not the one intended.
One review looked at research on preventing sexual harm in nightlife. People given victim-focused tips went on to blame victims MORE than people given tips aimed at potential perpetrators.
So this page is built the other way around: what you can do for other people, what actually reduces risk, and what to do afterwards.

sources.name: Button et al., Archives of Sexual Behavior 2024

spiking.headline: Drink spiking, honestly
spiking.blurb: Not what the posters say, and the products sold for it mostly do not work.

items.t: The drug most likely to be involved is alcohol
items.d: A US study looked at 144 people reporting sexual assault. Drugs were found in 61.8%. Only 4.9% were the classic “date-rape” drugs. In 4.2%, the person was assessed as having been drugged without knowing.
items.note: This is not a reason to relax. It is a reason to point your attention at the right thing — how much you have actually had, and who is topping you up.

sources.name: Negrusz et al., NIJ 2005
Dalaker et al., PLoS One 2024

items.t: Drink test strips and coasters mostly do not work
items.d: Detection coasters found ketamine 0% of the time in lab testing. Their “GHB” reagent turned out to be bromocresol green. That is a pH indicator. It responds to any drink above about pH 5.5, not to GHB.
items.note: Massachusetts' health department reviewed these and recommended against buying and distributing them. California, meanwhile, requires bars to offer them — and in the same law immunizes everyone against a wrong result. A state mandate is not an efficacy finding.

sources.name: Germain et al., Forensic Sci Int 2023
Gautam & Grela, Anglia Ruskin University for Drinkaware, 2024

items.t: A cover is different, and worth using
items.d: Nobody has tested whether drink covers work — that is a real gap, not a hidden finding. But a cover cannot give you a false negative. A strip can tell you your drink is clear when it is not, and that is worse than having nothing.
items.note: That distinction is the whole point: prefer the thing that cannot lie to you.

items.t: If you think it happened
items.d: Urine is worth collecting up to 96 hours after. That is longer than most sources say. Sooner is much better, and the first time you pee is the best sample.
items.note: Voluntary drug use does not make it not an assault, and does not disqualify a case. The federal examination protocol says so directly to clinicians.

sources.name: US DOJ — National Protocol for Sexual Assault Medical Forensic Examinations

items.t: And the other direction
items.d: In a survey of 6,064 students, 462 reported having been drugged — and 83 reported drugging someone else. Men who did it most often gave “having fun” as the reason. Giving somebody a drug they are not expecting is never a joke, whatever it was.

sources.name: Swan et al., Psychology of Violence 2017

items.t: Condoms, and what actually breaks them
items.d: About 98% effective used perfectly, and around 87% in real life. That means roughly 13 of every 100 people using them as their only birth control get pregnant in a year.
items.note: New one every time, on before any genital contact, pinch the air out of the tip, hold the base coming out. Not in a wallet, not two at once, never past the expiry.

items.t: Oil destroys latex, fast
items.d: Mineral oil cut condom strength by around 90% after sixty seconds of contact. Baby oil dropped the average burst time from nearly a minute to just over eleven seconds. Water- or silicone-based only, with latex AND with polyisoprene. Polyurethane is the exception that tolerates oil.
items.note: Lambskin is for pregnancy only — its pores are more than ten times the diameter of HIV.

items.t: Internal condoms, and one hard rule
items.d: About 95% with perfect use, around 79% typical. They can be used for anal sex, though the evidence for that specifically is described as unknown. Used at the same time as an external condom, the friction tears both.

items.t: Dental dams
items.d: The CDC recommends them and gives instructions, including how to cut one from a condom. Worth saying plainly: nobody has ever measured how much risk they remove. We are not going to borrow a condom's number for them.

items.t: Long sessions
items.d: Friction over hours causes sores and bleeding, which is how HIV and hepatitis get passed on during sessions that were meant to be safe. Plenty of water-based lube, and a new condom every 30 minutes rather than every act.

sources.name: We Are With You — chemsex harm reduction
CDC — condom use resources
Voeller et al., Contraception 1989

items.t: PEP is an emergency, and the clock is 72 hours
items.d: If you think you were exposed to HIV — sex, a shared needle, an assault — post-exposure prophylaxis works if started within 72 hours, ideally within 24. It is a 28-day course. Go to an emergency room or urgent care and say you need PEP. It is started before any test results come back — the 72-hour clock matters more than the confirmation does.
items.note: In twelve states pharmacists can prescribe it directly: Arkansas, California, Colorado, Illinois, Maine, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Utah and Virginia.

sources.name: CDC — nPEP guidelines, MMWR 2025

items.t: PrEP, and how long before it protects you
items.d: Daily pills, a shot every two months, or a shot twice a year. Around 99% risk reduction from sex and at least 74% for injecting. It is not immediate: roughly 7 days of daily pills for receptive anal sex, and around 21 days for receptive vaginal sex and for injecting.
items.note: CDC does not recommend the on-demand “2-1-1” schedule — it is not FDA approved and there is no data for people who inject, for women, or for trans people.

sources.name: CDC — PrEP

items.t: Recreational drugs do not interfere with most PrEP
items.d: This is the reassuring one and it is real: there are no known interactions between recreational drugs and the daily PrEP pills or the shot every two months. The exception is the twice-yearly lenacapavir shot, which does affect how the body clears other drugs.

sources.name: aidsmap — interactions between HIV medication and recreational drugs

items.t: Testing, and how often
items.d: Men who have sex with men: test for syphilis, chlamydia and gonorrhea at least once a year. Test at every site of contact, condom or not. With several partners, every 3 to 6 months. That includes while you are on PrEP.

sources.name: CDC — STI testing

items.t: What you can get, and by when
items.d: Levonorgestrel (Plan B and generics) is over the counter with no age limit and no ID, and works best within 72 hours. Ulipristal (ella) needs a prescription and works up to 120 hours. A copper IUD fitted within 120 hours is the most effective option there is — better than 99% — and works as well on day five as day one.

items.t: The one thing everybody agrees on about body weight
items.d: Whether the pills work less well at higher body weights is genuinely unsettled. One US label mentions it only deep inside its clinical studies, not as a warning. The European regulator looked at the same evidence in 2014 and deleted its weight statements. And the study behind the numbers people quote was small.
items.note: If levonorgestrel is what you can actually get hold of, take it. Taking it beats not taking it.

items.t: Two things that stop it working
items.d: Two different kinds of morning-after pill within five days of each other can cancel each other out. And enzyme-inducing medicines reduce it: rifampin, St. John's wort, carbamazepine, phenytoin, topiramate and some HIV medicines.
items.note: There is no evidence that recreational drugs affect it either way, because nobody has studied it. The documented risk is prescribed medicines and St. John's wort, which is sold over the counter.

sources.name: EMA — levonorgestrel and ulipristal remain suitable regardless of bodyweight (2014)
FDA — Plan B One-Step information
ACOG — emergency contraception FAQ

interactions.headline: The combinations that put people in the hospital

items.t: Poppers and erection pills
items.d: Both drop blood pressure, and together they can drop it catastrophically. The FDA labels contraindicate nitrites outright. After tadalafil (Cialis) allow at least 48 hours. After sildenafil (Viagra) the label says the safe interval is unknown, even at 24 hours.
items.note: Swallowing poppers rather than inhaling is a hospital emergency, not something to sleep off — it turns blood brown and starves it of oxygen. Blue or gray lips with breathlessness after someone drank from a small bottle is a 911 call.

sources.name: DailyMed — VIAGRA label
DanceSafe — poppers

items.t: Boosted HIV medication and MDMA
items.d: If your regimen contains ritonavir or cobicistat, it slows how your body clears MDMA — one clinician guide puts it at five to ten times, and says avoid. The evidence is case reports rather than trials, but one of them was fatal and another nearly so.
items.note: Look at what you actually take. Boosters are in darunavir, atazanavir, Kaletra, Stribild, Genvoya, Symtuza, Prezcobix and Evotaz. Bictegravir and dolutegravir regimens without a booster do not do this.

sources.name: NY/NJ AIDS Education and Training Center — recreational drugs and antiretrovirals

items.t: GHB and GBL — the margin is the problem
items.d: The dose people want and the dose that stops breathing are only about five times apart. And it is usually measured by eye, out of a squeeze bottle.
items.note: GBL can be two to three times stronger than GHB by volume, so swapping one for the other at the same amount is an overdose. A marked oral syringe measures it; two hours is the usual gap before redosing. Alcohol, benzos, ketamine and meth stack with it — the depressant effects add up, and that combination is where most GHB overdoses come from. Withdrawal from regular use can start within hours of the last dose and bring on seizures and delirium that need a hospital — do not stop abruptly alone.

sources.name: Le & Richards, StatPearls — GHB toxicity
DanceSafe — GHB

testing.headline: Getting tested
testing.blurb: Free testing exists in most of the country, and the part people get wrong is not where — it is when.

items.t: Testing too early tells you about last year, not last week
items.b: For HIV, the wait depends on the test. A lab nucleic-acid test can find it 10 to 33 days after. A lab antigen/antibody test, 18 to 45 days. A rapid finger-stick or at-home antibody test, 23 to 90 days.

items.t: Which test you get is not the same question as how fast you get it
items.b: An at-home antibody test is the slowest to close its window and the easiest to actually do. A clinic drawing blood from a vein closes it soonest. If something happened recently, the useful move is often to test now for a baseline and again after the window, rather than picking one moment and hoping.

items.t: Free is normal, not a favor
items.b: Health departments, Planned Parenthood, syringe service programs, and many community clinics test at no cost, and a lot of them do not ask for insurance or an ID. Mail-in kits exist too. None of it is conditional on stopping using.

items.t: If you inject, ask for hepatitis C as well
items.b: It is not on a standard STI panel and has to be asked for. It transmits through shared equipment far more readily than through sex, and the app's other pages assume the injecting route rather than this one.

sources.name: CDC — HIV testing and window periods
CDC — find free and low-cost testing near you

after.headline: After a positive result
after.blurb: Most of what people fear here is either fixable or already over by the time they are told.

items.t: Chlamydia, gonorrhea and syphilis are cured with antibiotics
items.b: Not managed — cured. Treatment is usually a single injection or a short course. What matters afterwards is not having sex until treatment is finished and any partner is treated too, or you hand it back and forth.

items.t: Get retested at three months, not to check the cure
items.b: CDC advises retesting about three months after treatment for chlamydia or gonorrhea. That is not doubt about whether the antibiotics worked — reinfection from an untreated partner is common, and it is the most likely thing a follow-up finds.

items.t: You can tell a partner without telling them who you are
items.b: Health departments run partner services that will notify someone anonymously, and free sites will send an anonymous text or email for you. Nobody has to hear it from you directly for them to get treated.

items.t: Hepatitis C is curable, and using is not a reason to be refused
items.b: Eight to twelve weeks of tablets cure well over ninety per cent of cases. The joint AASLD and IDSA guidance is explicit that ongoing substance use is not a reason to withhold treatment, and studies of people actively injecting show high completion and cure rates. If a provider says you have to be abstinent first, that is their policy, not the standard of care.

items.t: HIV is treatable and treatment stops transmission
items.b: Someone on treatment with an undetectable viral load does not transmit HIV sexually. That is a settled finding, not an optimistic framing.

sources.name: AASLD/IDSA — HCV guidance: treat regardless of ongoing substance use
CDC — HIV testing and window periods

doxypep.headline: Doxy-PEP
doxypep.blurb: An antibiotic taken after sex to prevent bacterial STIs. Newer than most of this page, and not for everyone.

items.t: What it is
items.b: A single 200 mg dose of doxycycline taken within 72 hours after oral, vaginal or anal sex — no more than 200 mg in any 24 hours. In trials it cut syphilis and chlamydia by more than seventy per cent and gonorrhea by roughly half.

items.t: Who CDC recommends it for
items.b: Men who have sex with men, and transgender women, who have had syphilis, chlamydia or gonorrhea diagnosed in the past twelve months. That is the group the evidence covers.

items.t: Who it is not established for
items.b: Trials in cisgender women have not shown the same benefit, and there is not enough evidence for heterosexual men. That is an absence of proof rather than proof it does not work — it means the honest answer is a conversation with a prescriber, not this page.

items.t: It is prescribed, and it is not a substitute
items.b: You need a prescription, and it does nothing for HIV — PrEP is a separate thing that does that job. Doxycycline also makes some people burn more easily in the sun.

sources.name: CDC — Clinical guidelines on doxycycline postexposure prophylaxis, 2024
CDC — Preventing STIs with doxy-PEP

sitting.note: HAND-WRITTEN. Peer support for someone having a hard time on a drug — NOT overdose response. The boundary between the two is the most important thing in this file and is stated first, in a stop callout, because sitting with someone who actually needs an ambulance is how a survivable night becomes a death. Zendo's four principles are used with attribution; Fireside's number verified 2026-08-11.
sitting.headline: Sitting with someone having a hard time
sitting.intro: Most difficult experiences do not need a hospital. They need one calm person who stays. This is what that person actually does.

notThis.title: First: is this a hard time, or an emergency?
notThis.body: Stop reading and call 911 if any of these is true.
notThis.detail: None of what follows applies to any of that. Sitting with someone is for fear, confusion, panic and overwhelm — not for a body that is failing.
signs: Breathing is slow, stopped, or sounds like snoring or gurgling
Their skin is blue or gray
A seizure that does not stop, or a second one
Their body is very hot to touch and they are confused

principles.title: The four principles
principles.credit: From the Zendo Project, who have used this model with over 1,900 people at festivals and events since 2012.

items.name: Create a safe space
items.what: Somewhere quieter and dimmer than where they are now, with fewer people. Ask before you move them or touch them. Sit at their level rather than standing over them. Deal with the obvious physical things — water, a blanket, somewhere to sit down, a route to a bathroom.

items.name: Sit, don't guide
items.what: You are not steering the experience. Words often get in the way, so use fewer than feels natural. Do not analyze what is happening to them or explain what it means. Listen, and let silence be allowed.

items.name: Talk through, not down
items.what: Do not try to pull someone out of what they are feeling — help them go through it. "Tell me about it" beats "you're fine". Reassurance that dismisses the experience tends to make someone feel more alone in it, not less.

items.name: Difficult is not the same as bad
items.what: Frightening and painful experiences are not automatically harmful ones, and the way somebody is met while it happens changes how it lands afterwards. Panic in the room makes it worse; steadiness makes it survivable.

sources.name: Zendo Project — working with difficult psychedelic experiences
MAPS — the four principles

doing.title: What that looks like in practice

items.t: Say who you are, more than once.
items.b: Time and identity get slippery. "I'm Sam, we're at my place, you took something and it's making you feel strange, I'm staying with you" — repeated calmly whenever they need it — does more work than anything clever.

items.t: Give the feeling a shape and an end.
items.b: "This is the drug, and it will pass" is true, orienting, and worth saying often. If you know roughly how long the substance lasts, saying so helps.

items.t: Breathe with them, don't instruct them.
items.b: Sit close and slow your own breathing. People match it without being told. "Breathe!" as a command mostly reads as alarm.

items.t: Offer, never impose.
items.b: Water, a different room, a blanket, the lights lower, going outside. Ask; accept no. Someone who has lost their footing needs to be the one still making choices.

items.t: Keep your own face calm.
items.b: In an altered state people read expressions far more than sentences. If you look frightened, they will believe there is something to be frightened of.

items.t: Stay until it is over, and a while after.
items.b: The tail is where people are left alone. It is also when they are most likely to want to talk.

items.t: Don't argue with what they are seeing or feeling.
items.b: You cannot win, and trying makes you an opponent instead of an anchor.

items.t: Don't crowd them.
items.b: A ring of concerned faces reads as an audience or a threat. One or two people, maximum.

items.t: Don't give them more drugs to fix it.
items.b: Including alcohol and including a benzodiazepine that is not theirs. It adds an unknown to a situation that already has too many.

items.t: Don't threaten them with hospital or police to get compliance.
items.b: It escalates fear at the exact moment fear is the problem — and it teaches them not to tell anyone next time.

items.t: Don't leave them alone to "sleep it off".
items.b: This is the single most common way a hard time turns into an emergency nobody witnessed.

items.t: Don't make it about how worried you were.
items.b: That conversation is legitimate, and it belongs to a later day.

overamping.title: If it's a stimulant, not a psychedelic
overamping.body: Overamping — too much stimulant — looks different: racing heart, chest tightness, overheating, paranoia, jaw clenching, hours without sleep. The sitting principles still apply, and a few physical things matter more: get them somewhere cool, keep water going in small amounts rather than large, and get them off their feet.
overamping.warn: Overheating is the part that becomes medical. A body that is very hot, with confusion, is an emergency — not something to sit through.

lines.name: Fireside Project
lines.what: Free peer support by phone or text, during or after a psychedelic experience. Anonymous. You can hand them the phone.

lines.name: Never Use Alone
lines.what: Stays on the line and sends help if someone stops responding. For opioids, not psychedelics.

lines.name: Poison Control
lines.what: Free, 24/7, confidential. They answer "is this dangerous" questions without involving police.

after.title: Afterwards
after.body: Let them sleep, and check on them the next day. A difficult experience someone was accompanied through often settles into something they can make sense of; the same experience gone through alone tends not to. If they want to talk about it, listening is still the whole job — you do not need to interpret it for them.

stimulants.note: Hand-curated. Sleep loss and psychosis are covered together because they arrive together. Where the evidence cannot separate the drug from the sleep, the page says so rather than picking one.
stimulants.headline: Staying up, and coming down
stimulants.blurb: What days without sleep do on their own, what stimulant psychosis actually looks like, how to help somebody in it, and what it costs to call for help.

sleep.headline: What being awake does by itself
sleep.lead: None of the studies below involved drugs. This is what sleep loss alone does to a healthy person.

items.t: Hours awake convert into something like being drunk
items.d: Forty people were kept awake 28 hours in one condition and given alcohol in another. After 17 hours awake, performance matched a blood alcohol level of 0.05%. After 24 hours awake, it matched roughly 0.10% — over the legal limit everywhere in the US. A second study of 39 people found the same thing independently.
items.note: This is not about willpower. The impairment happens whether or not you feel impaired.

sources.name: Dawson & Reid, Nature 1997
Williamson & Feyer, Occup Environ Med 2000

items.t: You stop being able to tell
items.d: 48 adults were held to restricted sleep for two weeks. The people on six hours and the people on four hours rated their own sleepiness about the same. Their actual performance kept getting further apart.

sources.name: Van Dongen et al., Sleep 2003

items.t: Everything gets bigger
items.d: After about 35 hours awake, the brain's threat center responded roughly 60% more strongly to unpleasant images, with the connection to the part that normally regulates it weakened. Small things stop feeling small. That is measurable, not a character flaw.

sources.name: Yoo et al., Current Biology 2007

hallucination.headline: Sleep loss alone will do this eventually
hallucination.lead: A review of 21 studies covering 760 people, all of them healthy, none of them on drugs, found a consistent timeline.

stages.d: Perceptual distortions, anxiety, irritability, feeling detached from yourself, losing track of time.
Delusions. At this point the review describes the picture as resembling acute psychosis.

body: It happened in 20 of the 21 studies. How many people it happens to varies enormously. In one large study of army recruits at 112 hours awake it was about 1 in 9. In some smaller ones it was everybody.
It is worst around 4am. Time awake matters, but so does what time it is.
Recovery took roughly half as long as the time spent awake. Most people were fine after sleeping. In five of the studies, some people were still confused or having odd thoughts days or weeks later.
hallucination.note: So: if you have been up three days and things are getting strange, that is not necessarily the drug, and it is not you going mad permanently. It is a documented effect of not sleeping, and sleep is the treatment.

sources.name: Waters et al., Frontiers in Psychiatry 2018 (21 studies, 760 people)

interaction.headline: Sleep loss and stimulants together — what is actually known
body: This is where honest reporting matters, because the obvious answer is not the proven one.

Methamphetamine on its own produces psychotic symptoms, and more of it means more symptoms. In 278 people tracked across more than a thousand months, symptoms were there in 25% of months. The odds rose sharply with the number of days used that month.
One study compared people who developed amphetamine psychosis with people who used and did not. The psychosis group had been awake longer. They had also used more, and no study separates those two.
interaction.note: We are telling you this because sleep is one of the few things in reach. Treat it as worth protecting, not as a proven cause you can point at afterwards.

sources.name: McKetin et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2013 (278 people, 1,064 person-months)
Arunogiri et al., Aust N Z J Psychiatry 2018 (systematic review)

items.t: Mostly it is being certain someone is after you
items.d: Across several inpatient studies, persecutory delusions were the most common feature — 77% of 168 people in one, 85% of 152 in another. Hearing things came next, in roughly half. Seeing things was less common, and feeling things on the skin was rarer than the “meth mites” stories suggest: in the study that counted it, 2 of 152.

sources.name: Srisurapanont et al., 2003 (N=168)
Zarrabi et al., 2016 (N=152)

items.t: Most of it passes quickly
items.d: Of 205 emergency department presentations with psychotic features, 170 resolved completely, 200 were handled without admission, and the median stay was 15 hours. In people sick enough to be admitted to a psychiatric ward it takes longer — of 152 inpatients, about 1 in 3 had not recovered within a month.
items.note: Which of those two pictures applies to you depends mostly on how bad it is when somebody looks at you, not on the drug.

items.t: It can be the first sign of something else
items.d: Across a meta-analysis of 50 studies covering 40,783 people, about 22% of amphetamine-induced psychoses were later diagnosed as schizophrenia. But a Swedish study of 7,606 people found the ones who converted were marked by inherited risk for psychosis — not by heavier drug use. Their conclusion was that this is a drug-precipitated illness in people already vulnerable, rather than one the drug creates from nothing.
items.note: Worth knowing in both directions: it does not mean you are destined for schizophrenia, and it does mean a first episode is worth telling a doctor about.

sources.name: Murrie et al., Schizophrenia Bulletin 2020
Kendler et al., 2019 (N=7,606)

helping.headline: Helping somebody who is in it
helping.lead: This is consensus guidance from emergency psychiatry, and the people who wrote it say plainly that the evidence base is thin. It is still the best there is, and most of it costs nothing.

items.t: One person talks
items.d: Not three. Several people talking at once is one of the reliable ways to make it worse. Everyone else steps back.

items.t: Two arms' length, hands visible
items.d: Stay far enough away that neither of you feels cornered, and make sure you can both leave. Stand at an angle rather than squared up. If they tell you to move, move immediately.

items.t: Short sentences, then wait
items.d: Simple words, one idea at a time, and leave a gap. Processing is slow right now.

items.t: Do not argue with the content
items.d: You do not have to agree that it is true, and you must not pretend to. What works is agreeing that they are experiencing it: you have never been through what they are going through, and you believe that they are going through it.

items.t: Offer real choices
items.d: A blanket, water, somewhere quieter, a phone call. Choice is the only power somebody has when they feel cornered — but only offer what you can actually deliver. Never promise something to calm them down that you cannot produce.

emergency.title: When it stops being a psychological emergency and becomes a medical one
emergency.body: Get help immediately for: a temperature you would call dangerous, confusion or unconsciousness, chest pain, a seizure, or a stroke sign. Overheating is the one on that list people die of, and it moves fastest — a body cannot stay that hot for long. Call 911, and cool them while you wait — cold water over as much skin as you can get to, re-wet constantly, with air moving over it. Not a cloth on the forehead. See Heat and water for the whole sequence.

sources.name: Richmond et al., Project BETA verbal de-escalation, West J Emerg Med 2012
National Harm Reduction Coalition — responding to overamping
