calling.headline: What calling for help actually costs
calling.lead: We are not going to tell you it is simple. Here is what the numbers say, so you can decide.

items.d: Emergency services were dispatched in about 2 in 100 calls. Across nearly two million calls, dispatch happened in about half of the calls where the counselor judged someone to be at imminent risk. Roughly half of those dispatches were without the person's agreement.

sources.name: Vibrant Emotional Health — imminent risk data

items.t: 911 for a stimulant overdose
items.d: In one large US city across two years, 21% of stimulant-involved overdose responses were followed by the person being jailed within six hours — against 9% for opioid-involved ones. That is one city, and it is the only measurement of its kind we could find.

sources.name: Ray et al., Drug Alcohol Depend 2022

items.t: Good Samaritan laws do not cover this
items.d: All 50 states and DC have them now — Wyoming was the last, in 2025 — but they are written for drug overdose, not for psychiatric crisis. They mostly do not cover outstanding warrants, and they generally protect against minor drug charges only.
items.note: Nobody has ever studied what happens when someone calls for help specifically for drug-induced psychosis. We are naming that gap rather than filling it with reassurance.

sources.name: Network for Public Health Law — overdose Good Samaritan laws

calling.note: None of this is a reason to let somebody overheat or stop breathing. It is a reason to know what you are choosing, and to make the call anyway when it is that kind of emergency.

items.t: The shape of it
items.d: Across three small inpatient studies, the worst is in the first 24 hours and eases over roughly the first week, with a longer tail of at least a couple more weeks. Depression and psychotic symptoms tend to lift within about a week. Anxiety and craving do not follow that curve — craving in one study did not drop until the second week.
items.note: Those studies were all in supervised settings with a bed and food. Crashing alone is harder than the numbers suggest.

items.t: Nothing you can take makes it shorter
items.d: A Cochrane review found four randomized trials with 125 people between them and concluded no medication is effective for amphetamine withdrawal. There is no evidence for melatonin, for antihistamines, or for benzodiazepines here.
items.note: Benzodiazepines carry a specific risk here. Fentanyl does turn up in the stimulant supply. In samples tested it has run around 6 to 15% for powder cocaine and powder meth, and under 2% for crack and crystal. And a benzodiazepine plus an opioid is how people stop breathing.

sources.name: Cochrane — treatment for amphetamine withdrawal

items.t: Water is not an antidote
items.d: Stimulants and MDMA both stop your body clearing water properly. Every year people drink far past that, believing it will fix a bad experience, and swell their brain. A splitting headache, confusion and vomiting are the early signs.

sources.name: Hew-Butler et al. — 3rd International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus (2015)
Atila et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024 — MDMA and hyponatremia

supervision.note: Hand-curated. Nothing here explains how to beat a test — that is out of scope on purpose. This is about understanding what you are facing and what you are actually entitled to.
supervision.headline: Drug testing, probation and parole
supervision.blurb: What a test can and cannot see, what to do when it says something wrong, and what the law says about being on methadone or buprenorphine while under supervision.

rights.headline: A positive screen is not a result yet
body: Almost every test starts as an immunoassay — a fast, cheap, presumptive screen. It is not an identification. It reacts to a shape, which is why it can be set off by things you did not take and miss things you did.
The confirmation is a different machine: GC/MS or LC-MS/MS, which identifies the actual molecule. Labs do not always run it unless somebody asks.

callout.title: On federal supervision, contesting it is what triggers confirmation
callout.body: Federal law requires a confirmed result before a screen can cost you your liberty. The courts' own guide says it plainly: if an instant screen is positive and you contest it, the sample has to be sent for GC/MS confirmation.

rights.caveat: State probation and parole rules vary, and we have not checked them state by state. Ask your attorney or public defender what your state requires. Ask before you need it.

sources.name: 18 U.S.C. § 3583 — supervised release
18 U.S.C. § 3563 — conditions of probation

panels.headline: What is actually on the test
panels.blurb: A panel only finds what it was built to look for. Several of the drugs most present in the supply are on no routine panel at all.

items.t: Fentanyl is not on a classic 5-panel
items.d: The standard five — amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis, opiates, PCP — does not include it. Fentanyl has no structural resemblance to morphine, so morphine-calibrated opiate assays do not react to it. It needs its own assay. Federal agency testing added a dedicated fentanyl line effective July 7 2025; DOT-regulated testing still has not, as of August 2026.

items.t: Xylazine is on nothing routine
items.d: Absent from both federal panels. A dedicated xylazine immunoassay exists but is labeled for forensic use, not clinical. If somebody wants to know whether xylazine is involved, it has to be asked for specifically.

items.t: Methadone and buprenorphine need their own assays
items.d: Neither is on the federal panel and neither cross-reacts with the opiate screen. Being prescribed one does not make you show up positive for opioids, and a routine panel will not confirm you are taking it either.

items.t: Gabapentin, kratom and most novel benzos are invisible by default
items.d: Novel benzodiazepines depend on the assay. A benzodiazepine screen will often flag etizolam or flualprazolam, sometimes several times more sensitively than its own calibrator. A negative screen does not rule out bromazolam.

sources.name: Federal Register 91 FR 12308 — current HHS testing cutoffs (March 13 2026)

windows.headline: How long it stays in you
windows.blurb: Urine, because that is what almost every test uses. Every figure carries the study it came from — a window without its conditions is not a fact.
windows.lead: Three things decide the answer far more than the drug does: how much and how long you have been using, what threshold the lab set, and which machine they ran. The same drug can give wildly different answers on all three.

method.title: The method matters more than most people are told
method.body: Eighteen people were given one 0.4 mg dose of buprenorphine. On the immunoassay it was detectable for a mean of 9 hours. On LC-MS/MS, from the identical dose in the same people, a mean of 76 hours. Its metabolite was still positive in every single person when the study ended at 96 hours. Same drug, same dose, same bodies — the machine set the window.

sources.name: Kronstrand et al., J Anal Toxicol 2008 (N=18)

rows.urine: Roughly half a day to 5½ days for fentanyl itself; its metabolite norfentanyl ran 2.7 to 10.7 days. A separate group of 12 people entering treatment averaged 7.3 days for fentanyl and 13.3 for norfentanyl — one person was still positive at 19 and 26 days.
rows.note: Far longer than the two to four days people expect from short-acting opioids. If you are being tested after switching off fentanyl, this is the number to know.

rows.urine: The heroin-specific marker (6-MAM) is gone fast — often within 8 hours. Morphine itself is 1 to 3 days for occasional use; in 52 chronic users the average was 4.95 days and the longest 11.3 days at a sensitive cutoff.
1 to 14 days. Many methadone assays detect only the parent drug and not its metabolite EDDP — which is why EDDP testing is what distinguishes actually taking it from a sample it was added to.
4 to 24 hours by immunoassay; 23 to 96 hours by mass spectrometry. See above — the difference is the machine, not you.
Short-acting ones around 3 days. Long-acting, in chronic use, up to 30 days. Alprazolam runs 1 to 5 days and clonazepam 1 to 12.
rows.note: But see the section above: alprazolam, lorazepam and clonazepam frequently do not show up at all on a standard screen, whatever the window.

rows.urine: Measured as its metabolite. In 18 chronic users during monitored cessation the average last positive was 57.5 hours, with the longest at 147 hours — a little over 6 days.
Highly cutoff-dependent. In controlled dosing, dropping to the lower of two common thresholds extended detection by up to 24 hours for methamphetamine and up to 34 hours overall.
rows.note: Prescribed amphetamine can sometimes be told apart from illicit by testing which mirror-image form is there. We could not verify any threshold a lab uses to make that call. Do not assume it will be done.

rows.urine: The widest range of anything here, and the most cutoff-dependent. The same frequent users in one study were positive for 17, 22 or 27 days depending purely on which of three thresholds was applied. In 60 people on a closed unit, grouped by starting concentration, the average last positive was 4.3, 9.7 or 15.4 days.
rows.note: Published maximums are floors, not ceilings — several of these studies ended while people were still testing positive.

rows.urine: Its metabolite norketamine was detectable up to 14 days by the most sensitive method in one hospital study, and ketamine itself up to 11 days. One child in that study never tested positive at all across 16 days.
40 to 130 hours to fall below a common cutoff, median 78, in 32 people in detox. But see hand sanitizer above — EtG at these thresholds does not distinguish drinking from incidental exposure.
Roughly half a day to 5 days in urine. Not on any routine panel, so it will only be found if someone specifically looks.
1 to 2 days. Not on the federal panel.

gaps.title: What we could not verify, and are not going to guess
items: MDMA. We found no controlled-dosing source we could actually read, in any matrix. Rather than repeat a number off a rehab marketing page, there is nothing here.
Blood, saliva and hair windows for most of these drugs. Urine is well studied; the others largely are not, and the tables that circulate for them are mostly unsourced.
Kratom, and most novel benzodiazepines. No commercial cutoffs we could confirm at source.

sources.name: Bird et al., Am J Addict 2025 — fentanyl and xylazine urine windows
Huhn et al., Drug Alcohol Depend 2020 — fentanyl in treatment entry
Preston et al., J Anal Toxicol 2002 — cocaine during cessation
Oyler et al., Clin Chem 2002 — methamphetamine controlled dosing
Adamowicz & Kala, J Anal Toxicol 2005 — ketamine
Helander et al., Alcohol Alcohol 2009 — urinary EtG
ARUP Consult — drug half-lives and urine detection windows

windows.perDrugNote: Urine, and only as a range — how much you used, for how long, which threshold the lab set and which machine they ran all move this more than the drug does.

misreads.headline: When the test is wrong
misreads.blurb: Both directions happen, and both are documented.

items.t: Hand sanitizer can produce a positive alcohol test
items.d: In one study, 11 people used ethanol hand sanitizer through the day for three days and drank nothing. Their urine EtG reached 2,001 ng/mL. That is four times the cutoff most labs use, and twenty times the sensitive clinical one.

sources.name: Reisfield et al., J Anal Toxicol 2011

items.t: Your prescribed benzodiazepine may not show up
items.d: Most benzodiazepine immunoassays are built around oxazepam or nordiazepam. Alprazolam and lorazepam are excreted mainly as glucuronides and are not detected unless the lab does an extra hydrolysis step, which most do not. Clonazepam becomes 7-aminoclonazepam, which barely cross-reacts. A negative screen is not evidence you stopped taking what you were prescribed.

sources.name: Moeller et al., Mayo Clin Proc 2017

items.t: Ordinary medicines set off the methadone screen
items.d: Verapamil, diphenhydramine and doxylamine are documented causes of methadone false positives. Diphenhydramine is Benadryl; doxylamine is in night-time cold medicine and some sleep aids.

sources.name: Moeller et al., Mayo Clin Proc 2017

cannabis.headline: Testing negative then positive is a known pattern
body: This is the one most likely to be used against you, and it is the one most people cannot argue their way out of without knowing it.

Cannabis does not leave the body on a smooth downward curve. Under strictly supervised abstinence — where continued use was ruled out by the study design — people alternated between positive and negative results for weeks. In a study of 60 people on a closed research unit, 40% did not reach their peak concentration until up to 2.9 days AFTER abstinence began.
So a negative followed by a positive is a documented excretion pattern in people who have not used. It is not proof of anything.

How long you stay positive depends enormously on the cutoff, which is why any single number is close to meaningless without one attached. The same frequent users in the same study were positive for 17 days at one threshold, 22 at a lower one, and 27 at a lower one still.
cannabis.note: Most chronic users clear faster than the famous long-tail figures suggest — but in one study of 37 people, roughly one in four were still above the cutoff after two weeks. Both things are true.

sources.name: Goodwin et al., J Anal Toxicol 2008 (N=60, 6,158 specimens)
Smith-Kielland et al., J Anal Toxicol 1999
Ellis et al., Clin Pharmacol Ther 1985 (N=86, supervised abstinence)

medication.headline: They cannot make you stop your medication
body: If you are prescribed methadone or buprenorphine, a court, a probation officer, a drug court or a jail telling you to taper off it is on very weak legal ground.

Federal law says so directly: medication taken under the supervision of a licensed health care professional is not “illegal use of drugs”. That is the statute, not a guideline — and the Americans with Disabilities Act covers courts, prisons and jails.

The Justice Department settled with Pennsylvania's court system in January 2024 over exactly this. It settled with the Massachusetts Parole Board in 2021, over a person being pushed onto a different medication than the one that was working.

callout.title: If it is happening to you
callout.body: Tapering because you were told to carries the most risk of any option here. Stopping medication is the single biggest overdose risk there is. And the order is on weak legal ground to start with.

medication.caveat: The Justice Department's guidance document says on its face that it does not carry the force of law. The statute it rests on does. Cite the statute.

links.name: DOJ — the ADA and people in treatment for opioid use disorder

sources.name: 42 U.S.C. § 12210(d) — medication under supervision is not illegal use

violations.headline: What a violation actually is
violations.blurb: Most people sent back are not sent back for a new crime.

items.t: Technical violations are the bulk of it
items.d: In 2021, 44% of state prison admissions came from probation or parole violations. Technical violations alone are nearly a quarter of every admission to state prison. Those are things like a missed appointment or a failed drug test.

sources.name: CSG Justice Center — Confined and Costly (2021 admissions data)

items.t: Calling 911 may not protect you from a violation
items.d: 27 states and DC extend Good Samaritan protection to probation and parole violations. 23 do not. And in Minnesota and North Carolina the statutes expressly preserve the authority to drug test you anyway — meaning the call itself is protected but the test that follows it is not. That is a real trap and worth knowing before the night it matters.

sources.name: LAPPA — Good Samaritan laws, July 2025

reentry.headline: The first two weeks after release are the most dangerous
body: Tolerance falls fast during any break in use, and jail or prison is a break in use. The dose that was normal before is not normal now.

In a study following 30,237 people released from Washington State prisons, the risk of fatal overdose in the first two weeks after release was 129 times that of the general population. A later North Carolina study, covering 2016 to 2018, found overdose deaths in the first two weeks after release at 46.6 times the expected rate.
Those numbers turn on three things. Naloxone in your hand on day one. Somebody else in the room. And an amount well below what used to be normal, because your tolerance changed, not the drug.

sources.name: Binswanger et al., N Engl J Med 2007
Ranapurwala et al., Am J Public Health 2022

hair.headline: If they use a hair test
body: Hair testing has problems the government's own proposed rule concedes.

It cannot see recent use at all — drugs do not appear in hair for 5 to 7 days after they are taken. And the first centimeter of hair does not represent the last month: because of the time it takes hair to reach the surface, it represents roughly one to two months ago.

A federal proposal published in September 2020 — still not finalized six years later, so it binds nobody today — would not let a hair result stand alone. An agency choosing to test hair must also collect another specimen type, and the rule cites litigation warning that action taken on a hair test alone may be legally vulnerable.

bias.title: It is not the same test for everyone
bias.body: In a study where 44 people took an identical controlled dose of codeine, the amount ending up in their hair tracked hair melanin — the correlation explained about 73% of the variance. Concentrations in black hair were around seven times those in brown and fourteen to fifteen times those in blond. At the cutoff the government proposes, 100% of the black-haired subjects would have been reported positive and only half of the brown-haired ones. Same drug, same dose, different hair.

sources.name: Rollins et al., J Anal Toxicol 2003 (N=44)

hair.thc: A controlled study found them in hair that had already grown before the person took anything. It also found them in people who had not used at all. It came from hands, sweat and smoke from someone who had.

sources.name: HHS proposed hair testing guidelines, 85 FR 56108
Moosmann et al., Scientific Reports 2015

support.reviewNote: Tone here matters more than completeness. This sits inside a harm reduction tool: it is for someone curious about options, never a push to quit, and never a judgment on anyone still using. Nothing should read as a condition for deserving help. Every link and phone number was verified 2026-08-10 — see EVIDENCE.md for what was checked and what was rejected.

body: Maybe you want to stop. Maybe you want to use less, or more safely. Maybe you want to keep using and just feel like a person again for a while. Maybe the thing you actually need help with is underneath all of it. Every one of those counts, and none of them is the wrong reason to be reading this.
You don’t have to be done using to ask for any of it. You don’t have to be sure, or have a plan, or have anything to show for the last six months.
framing.close: Nothing on this page is a judgment on how you’re living.

underneath.headline: What is often underneath
body: For a lot of people, substance use is not the first thing that happened. It is the thing that made something else survivable.

That is not an excuse, and it is not a diagnosis. It is a pattern, and the research on it is clear. It means the useful question is often not “how do I stop”. It is “what am I carrying, and what would help me put it down”.
underneath.note: Support for that exists separately from anything to do with drugs, and you can go looking for it without ever discussing your use.

options.intro: There are three medications for opioid use disorder. They are treatment, not a substitute addiction, and being on one is not a lesser kind of recovery.

medications.name: Buprenorphine (Suboxone, Sublocade)
medications.what: A partial opioid agonist. It has a ceiling effect, which is why it carries a much lower overdose risk than the opioids it replaces.
medications.how: Any clinician with a normal DEA registration can prescribe it — a regular doctor, a clinic, a community health center, telehealth, or an emergency room. It is filled at an ordinary pharmacy. The old special waiver was abolished in 2023 and there is no longer any cap on how many patients a prescriber can treat.
medications.note: Usually started when you are already in mild withdrawal, to avoid precipitated withdrawal. Ask about low-dose initiation if that is a barrier for you.

sources.name: SAMHSA — buprenorphine

medications.name: Methadone
medications.what: A full agonist, long acting, and the most studied of the three. It works for many people for whom buprenorphine does not.
medications.how: Only through a licensed opioid treatment program — that restriction is federal law, not a medical judgment about you. Find one through SAMHSA's directory below.
medications.note: Take-home rules loosened for good in 2024. Up to 7 days of take-homes in the first two weeks. Up to 14 through the first month. Up to 28 days after that. It is your clinician's judgment now, not a fixed checklist.

sources.name: SAMHSA — methadone
SAMHSA — 42 CFR Part 8 FAQs

medications.name: Naltrexone (Vivitrol)
medications.what: A blocker rather than an opioid. Monthly injection or daily pill. Any prescriber can order it.
medications.how: Requires being fully off opioids for roughly 7 to 10 days first.
medications.note: That gap is a real barrier and a real risk — tolerance drops during it, so a return to use in that window is more dangerous than usual. Worth weighing honestly against the other two.

sources.name: SAMHSA — naltrexone

evidence.body: A review of 15 trials and 36 studies covering more than 700,000 people found that while someone is on methadone or buprenorphine, overdose deaths and deaths from all causes drop sharply. In the four weeks after stopping, all-cause mortality was around six times higher, and stayed roughly double after that. The risk is not in taking the medication. It is in the weeks right after stopping — which is worth knowing if anyone pressures you to taper before you are ready.

sources.name: Santo et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2021

stimulants.body: It is mostly funded through state Medicaid programs, so it depends where you live. California, Delaware, Hawaii, Montana and Washington had approved programs as of early 2025. More may have been added since.

sources.name: SAMHSA TIP 33 — Treatment for Stimulant Use Disorders

getting.intro: Two national front doors, then the routes that work when you have no insurance and no money.

routes.name: SAMHSA National Helpline
routes.what: Free, confidential, 24/7, English and Spanish. They will not ask for your name or personal details — only a ZIP code. If you have no insurance they refer you to state-funded programs and sliding-scale providers. This is the fastest human route to care you can afford.

routes.name: FindTreatment.gov
routes.what: The government's treatment locator. Confidential and anonymous. Filter for medication treatment, payment options, and telehealth.

routes.name: Methadone program directory
routes.what: Methadone is only available through a licensed opioid treatment program. This is the official list.

routes.name: Community health centers
routes.what: Federally funded health centers are required to see you regardless of your ability to pay, on a sliding scale. Many prescribe buprenorphine. No insurance needed.

routes.name: Emergency departments can start you
routes.what: Many hospitals now start buprenorphine in the ER and connect you to a prescriber within a few days. In the programs built for this, treatment is not conditional on insurance, on lab results, or on promising to stop using anything else.
Dial 2-1-1 from anywhere in the US for local free and sliding-scale services — treatment, housing, food, transport.

routes.name: Medicaid
routes.what: There is no open enrollment period for Medicaid — you can apply any day of the year. Coverage rules vary by state, and some states can backdate coverage.

routes.name: If you are pregnant
routes.what: Fear of losing a child keeps many people away from care. A federal Plan of Safe Care is a health plan for you and the baby — it is not automatically a child protective services report. What is actually required varies a lot by state, and is often narrower than hospital practice suggests. This free toolkit covers your rights around drug testing, disclosure, and what happens after birth. Methadone and buprenorphine are the standard of care in pregnancy; being pregnant is not a reason to stop.

lines.name: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
lines.who: Call, text or chat 988 · Spanish: press 2 · ASL videophone available
lines.dispatch: They may send emergency services. Across nearly two million calls, that happened in about 2 in 100 — but in about half of the calls where the counselor judged someone to be at imminent risk. Roughly half of those dispatches were without the person's agreement.

lines.name: Never Use Alone
lines.who: Peer-run, 24/7. No abstinence requirement, no judgment. They stay on the line and send help if you stop responding.

lines.name: Veterans Crisis Line
lines.who: 988 then press 1, or text 838255. No VA enrollment needed.
lines.dispatch: Routes through 988, which may send emergency services without your agreement.

lines.name: Vet Centers
lines.who: Free, strictly confidential counseling at community storefronts kept separate from VA medical records. Combat, military sexual trauma in any era, and bereavement for families.

lines.name: The Trevor Project
lines.who: LGBTQ+ young people. Call, or text START to 678678.
lines.dispatch: In their own words, they “may need to contact a child welfare agency or emergency service.”

lines.name: Trans Lifeline
lines.who: Staffed by trans and nonbinary peers. Policy against calling police or emergency services without your explicit request.
lines.hours: Monday to Friday, 1pm–9pm Eastern. Closed weekends.

lines.name: StrongHearts Native Helpline
lines.who: For Native and Indigenous people. This is a domestic and sexual violence line — not a drug or overdose line.

lines.name: RAINN
lines.dispatch: In their own words, they are “required by law to report to authorities” in some circumstances.

lines.name: Childhelp
lines.who: Child abuse, including adult survivors. Call or text, 24/7.
lines.dispatch: A mandated-reporting line — they may contact child welfare or emergency services.

lines.name: Crisis Text Line
lines.dispatch: They may contact emergency services. Their policy is not stated in a way we could quote.

lines.name: Partnership to End Addiction
lines.who: Free, human-staffed support for families. Text CONNECT to 55753.

peer.intro: Groups differ enormously, and the differences are not always advertised at the door. The most important one is how a group treats people on medication.
peer.medicationNote: If you are on methadone or buprenorphine, this matters before you walk in. Some rooms will treat you as being in recovery without qualification. Others will not let you share or hold a position. You are entitled to know which is which in advance rather than finding out in front of a room.

groups.name: MARA — Medication-Assisted Recovery Anonymous
groups.what: Built specifically for people on medication. No abstinence requirement, no higher power.
groups.medication: Fully supported. This is the point of the group.

groups.name: SMART Recovery
groups.what: Secular, science-based, uses cognitive-behavioral tools. Your goal can be abstinence, moderation, or harm reduction.
groups.medication: Explicitly supported — SMART endorses legally prescribed addiction and psychiatric medication.

groups.name: LifeRing
groups.what: Secular, abstinence-based, no steps and no higher power.
groups.medication: Explicitly fine — their definition of sobriety carves out medically indicated prescribed medication.

groups.name: All Recovery meetings and recovery community centers
groups.what: Multi-pathway by design — 12-step, secular, medication and harm reduction people in the same room. Find your local recovery community organization and ask for their schedule.

groups.name: Narcotics Anonymous
groups.what: The largest and easiest to find. Abstinence-based and explicitly spiritual, though not tied to a religion.
groups.medication: NA as an organization takes no position on your medication and you are welcome to attend. But NA's own literature says individual groups may limit whether you can share or hold a service position, and warns you may meet strong opinions. NA's own advice is to try several meetings.

groups.name: Recovery Dharma
groups.what: Buddhist-informed, peer-governed, non-theistic — no higher power required. Abstinence is held as an intention.
groups.medication: No published position. Their current FAQ does not mention medication either way, so ask locally rather than assuming.

trauma.intro: You can get help with this without ever discussing drugs, and without deciding anything about your use first.

aces.title: What the research actually says
aces.body: A large study of childhood adversity found a stepwise pattern: the more categories of adversity someone reported, the higher their later risk. People reporting five or more were seven to ten times more likely to report drug problems, addiction, or injection drug use. That is one of the strongest patterns in public health.
aces.caveat: It describes populations, not people. One of the study's own lead authors published a correction warning that the score is being misused as if it were a screening or diagnostic tool. Your score is not a diagnosis, not a prognosis, and not a prediction about your life.

sources.name: Dube et al., Pediatrics 2003
Anda et al. — limits and misapplications

approaches.name: Seeking Safety
approaches.what: Present-focused coping skills for trauma and substance use at the same time. Does not require abstinence, and does not require retelling what happened. Worth asking for by name — many programs still make sobriety a condition of trauma treatment.

approaches.name: CPT (Cognitive Processing Therapy)
approaches.what: Around 12 sessions, working on the beliefs that formed afterwards — about blame, safety, and trust. A version exists that does not require a detailed account of the event.

approaches.name: Prolonged Exposure
approaches.what: Gradual, repeated approach to the memory and to avoided situations. Effective and demanding — dropping out is common, and deciding it is not for you is a legitimate choice.

approaches.name: EMDR
approaches.what: Attending to the memory while doing guided eye movements or other bilateral stimulation.

approaches.name: Somatic approaches
approaches.what: Body-based work, often experienced as gentler. Honest caveat: the evidence base is much smaller and earlier than the three above, and it is not among the strongly recommended treatments in current clinical guidelines.

experiences.name: Deciding between treatments
experiences.what: A free, non-commercial tool from the VA that compares trauma treatments side by side. No login, no sales.

experiences.name: Finding a therapist you can afford
experiences.what: Open Path connects uninsured and underinsured people to therapists at reduced rates.

experiences.name: Losing someone to an overdose
experiences.what: GRASP runs free peer groups, in person and online, specifically for people grieving a death from substances. Its sister organization does advocacy and naloxone education.

experiences.name: Losing a child, at any age
experiences.what: The Compassionate Friends is free and secular, with long-running online groups for overdose loss. Often the best option where there is no GRASP chapter.

experiences.name: Families of someone still using
experiences.what: Learn to Cope runs peer meetings for families, most weekdays online, including naloxone training.

experiences.name: Adult survivors of childhood abuse
experiences.what: Free peer-led groups and a free workbook.

experiences.name: Chronic pain, including anyone tapered against their will
experiences.what: The 2022 federal prescribing guideline was written partly to correct the misuse of the 2016 one. It states plainly that its recommendations are not rigid rules and should not lead to rapid tapering or abrupt discontinuation. If you were cut off, that was not what the guideline asked for.

experiences.name: Free self-help that is not a product
experiences.what: PTSD Coach from the VA, usable in a browser with nothing to install and nothing to sign up for. It does not replace care, and says so itself.

cost.headline: If you cannot pay
cost.body: Most of these routes have a version that needs no money and no paperwork. The SAMHSA line refers you to state-funded and sliding-scale programs without asking who you are. Community health centers cannot turn you away over money. Medicaid has no enrollment deadline.
cost.note: Community health centers are required to see people regardless of ability to pay.

supplies.intro: Naloxone, test strips, and safer-use supplies. Free options first, because most people reading this cannot pay and burying them under vendors is its own barrier.

free.name: NEXT Distro
free.what: Free naloxone by mail, discreetly packaged. Their state finder covers every state — where they cannot ship directly they hand you off to a program that can. This is the single best starting point if you are not sure where to look.

free.name: Your state health department
free.what: Many states mail free naloxone to any resident who asks, and some include fentanyl test strips. Which tier your state falls into is below.

free.name: Syringe service programs
free.what: SSPs give out naloxone, test strips, sterile supplies and wound care, usually with no ID and no questions. They are also the most reliable place to hear what is actually circulating locally.

directories.name: Harm Reduction Near You
directories.what: National Harm Reduction Coalition's directory of programs by location.

directories.name: NASEN syringe program directory
directories.what: The national list of syringe service programs.
Dial 2-1-1 and ask for harm reduction supplies or naloxone. Works everywhere, including where nothing above does.

paid.name: Naloxone over the counter
paid.what: Narcan 4 mg and RiVive 3 mg are available without a prescription at pharmacies nationwide. Worth knowing as a fallback, but check the free routes first — you should not have to pay for this.

paid.name: DanceSafe
paid.what: Reagent kits and fentanyl test strips. Their storefront moved to Transparency in March 2026; the strips are still made by the same manufacturer.

paid.name: BTNX
paid.what: The manufacturer of most fentanyl, xylazine, benzodiazepine and nitazene strips used in the US.

byState.intro: What your state offers, as of August 2026. This changes often — if your state is not in the first group, the NEXT Distro finder above still covers you.

tiers.label: Free naloxone AND test strips by mail, to any resident
Free naloxone by mail, no test strips
tiers.note: Some cap how many kits you can request, and Alaska ships only to Alaska addresses.

tiers.label: State program supplies organizations, not individuals
tiers.note: These states fund bulk naloxone for agencies and programs. As an individual, go through NEXT Distro or a local syringe service program instead — the state page will not help you directly.

tiers.label: No verified statewide mail program for individuals
tiers.note: Nonprofits often fill the gap. Hawaii's mail program covers Kauaʻi, Lānaʻi and Molokaʻi only, despite what most sources say.

closed.title: Recently closed — do not rely on these
items: Oklahoma discontinued its mail-order fentanyl test strip program, and the statewide naloxone vending machines were removed in September 2024.
Idaho repealed authorization for syringe service programs; all programs closed on June 30, 2024.
As of April 2026, federal grant money can no longer buy fentanyl or xylazine test strips. So state-funded strip programs are the likeliest listing here to disappear.

supplies.legalNote: Fentanyl test strips are legal in most states but not all, and xylazine strips are covered in fewer. Ordering by mail does not change your state's law. See the legality section on the Test tab before you order.

grassroots.intro: Programs run by and for people who use drugs. These often reach people the formal system turns away, ask for no ID and no story, and tend to know what is actually circulating locally weeks before any official alert does. Several also stay stocked when state programs run dry.

items.name: Grassroots Harm Reduction
items.what: A national network supporting local peer-run programs. Often the fastest route to free supplies where no storefront carries them — and they answer on social media when a website would be too slow.

items.name: National Survivors Union
items.what: The national union of drug users and sex workers, organized by people who use drugs — formerly Urban Survivors Union. Methadone advocacy, harm reduction education, an advocacy academy, and support for local and underground syringe programs. If there is no chapter where you are, they help you start one.
items.delivery: Local chapters, plus national online meetings

items.name: Never Use Alone
items.what: Peer-run, 24/7, staffed by people with lived experience. You give a location, they stay on the line, and they send help if you stop responding. No abstinence requirement and no judgment — verified from their own policy.

items.name: SafeSpot
items.what: Another peer-run overdose prevention line, expanding to more states.

items.name: Brave
items.what: Overdose detection hardware, built by peers. A button you press before you use alone, plus sensors for bathrooms and private rooms. Both are wired to a responder who checks on you.
items.cost: Devices are purchased, not free — configuration fee on a first order.
items.delivery: Devices, installed by a program or building

items.name: Remedy Alliance / For The People
items.what: Supplies naloxone in bulk at cost to harm reduction programs — much of the free naloxone handed out at a syringe program in the US passes through here. Not for individuals: if you run or volunteer with a program, this is where the supply comes from.

grassroots.note: Some community programs operate in legal gray areas depending on the state, which is exactly why they exist where official services do not. They will not ask you to explain yourself.

loved.headline: When it’s someone you love
loved.intro: Being close to someone who uses is its own kind of hard, and most of the advice people are handed makes things worse. What follows is what the research actually supports, not what feels decisive.

keeping.title: Keep the relationship. It is the thing that works.
keeping.body: It teaches communication and support instead of confrontation. Across randomized trials it reached about two-thirds of people whose families had been told nothing would work. Al-Anon-style facilitation reached about 13%. The confrontational “intervention” approach reached 23%.

sources.name: Meta-analysis of CRAFT trials (PubMed)
American Psychological Association — CRAFT
Partnership to End Addiction — what CRAFT is

does.t: Ask, then listen longer than is comfortable.
does.b: “How are you doing?” and then silence does more than any speech you have rehearsed. People tell you the real thing several minutes in, once they are sure you are not building toward a demand.

does.t: Say the specific thing you are worried about, once.
does.b: “I’ve noticed you’ve seemed really tired lately and I’m worried” lands. “You’re throwing your life away” does not. Say it plainly, then stop — repeating it turns concern into pressure.
It is often not what you assumed. Sometimes it is a ride, or money for strips, or somebody to text at 2am. Asking treats them as the expert on their own life, which they are.

does.t: Keep naloxone, and tell them you have it.
does.b: Not as a threat or a statement about them — as a fact about the house. Learn to use it. Ask them to teach you if they already know how.
This is the single most protective thing that does not require anyone to stop. Never Use Alone (1-800-484-3731) answers 24/7 and sends help if someone stops responding.

does.t: Notice out loud when things go well.
does.b: A day they seemed better, a thing they did, a plan they kept. Positive attention on the parts of life that are not about drugs is the mechanism CRAFT actually runs on — not a nicety.
You are allowed support that is about you, not about managing them. This is not selfish; the research finds it is part of what makes the rest sustainable.

donts.b: The televised “intervention” — surprise, ultimatums, a room of people — performs worse than simply keeping in contact, and can end the contact you still have.

donts.t: Don’t make love or contact conditional.
donts.b: “I’m done with you until you quit” removes the one thing keeping someone alive: another person who might notice. Cutting off contact pushes people toward using alone, and alone means nobody is there to give naloxone or call 911.

donts.t: Don’t set an ultimatum you will not keep.
donts.b: It teaches that what you say does not mean anything, and it puts you in the position of having to choose between your word and your person.

donts.t: Don’t treat abstinence as the only good outcome.
donts.b: Using less, using more safely, being alive in six months, staying in contact — those are real outcomes, and treating them as failure is how people stop telling you the truth.

donts.t: Don’t search their things or monitor them secretly.
donts.b: Once discovered — and it is discovered — you have traded the honesty you need for information you cannot act on.

donts.t: Don’t call it what the world calls it.
donts.b: “Addict”, “clean”, “junkie”: stigmatizing words measurably reduce how likely someone is to seek help, and they are the words your person has heard from every institution already.

hard.title: If they are not ready
hard.body: Most people are not, most of the time, and readiness is not something you can argue someone into. What you can do is stay someone they will call. The person who kept the door open is who people reach for when the moment does come — and that moment is far more often a quiet Tuesday than a rock bottom.

help.name: Partnership to End Addiction — free helpline and family coaching
help.note: Text, call, or email with a trained specialist. Free.

help.name: SMART Recovery Family & Friends
help.note: CRAFT-based meetings, online and in person.

pregnancy.headline: Pregnant, or parenting
pregnancy.intro: Written for the questions people actually ask, which are mostly legal and mostly about being reported. Nothing here is conditional on stopping, and none of it assumes what you have decided.

items.t: Stopping methadone or buprenorphine is the more dangerous option, not the safer one
items.b: Staying on it is the standard of care in pregnancy — ACOG, SAMHSA and ASAM all say so. Abrupt withdrawal carries a risk of fetal distress and pregnancy loss, and the relapse risk afterwards is the bigger danger of the two. If you are already on methadone, switching to buprenorphine is specifically warned against because of precipitated withdrawal. A provider who tells you to taper off to protect the pregnancy is going against the guidelines their own field wrote.

sources.name: ACOG — Opioid use and opioid use disorder in pregnancy
SAMHSA — Clinical guidance for treating pregnant and parenting women with opioid use disorder
ASAM — Opioid use disorder in pregnancy

items.t: A notification at birth is not a finding that you did anything
items.b: Federal law requires a hospital to notify child welfare when an infant is affected by substance use or withdrawal. That same law says plainly that the notification is not a finding of abuse or neglect.
items.note: Here is the part that really does depend on where you are. About half of states treat substance use in pregnancy as child abuse or neglect under their own law. A few allow civil commitment.

sources.name: Casey Family Programs — Plans of Safe Care
LAPPA — substance use during pregnancy, state by state

items.t: Whether you are tested, and whether you were asked, are separate questions
items.b: Testing practice at delivery varies by hospital and by state, and so does whether consent is sought for it. Some test on a written policy, some on a clinician's judgement, and the criteria used are documented to fall unevenly on poor and Black patients. You can ask what the policy is before you are in labor — a prenatal visit is a much better moment for that question than a delivery room.

items.t: Prenatal care is protective even if nothing else changes
items.b: The outcomes that get attributed to a drug are often the outcomes of no prenatal care, no nutrition and untreated infection. Going to appointments while still using improves things measurably. Programs exist that are built for exactly that and do not require abstinence to enrol.

sources.name: CDC — Opioid use and pregnancy

items.t: Withdrawal in a newborn is treatable, and you are usually part of the treatment
items.b: Neonatal opioid withdrawal is expected on stable medication, it is managed, and it is not brain damage. Rooming-in and skin-to-skin reduce how much medication the baby needs and how long they stay. Breastfeeding is generally encouraged on stable methadone or buprenorphine, with the usual exceptions. Being present is not a courtesy extended to you — it is part of the care.

sources.name: SAMHSA — Clinical guidance for treating pregnant and parenting women with opioid use disorder
CDC — Opioid use and pregnancy

items.t: If child services are already involved
items.b: Ask what specifically is being alleged and what the plan requires, in writing. A positive test is one fact and a plan is a list of tasks; they are not the same thing and the tasks are what you are actually measured against. Legal representation exists specifically for parents in these cases and it is usually free — ask the court for appointed counsel rather than going in alone.

pregnancy.gap: What this cannot tell you is your own state's law, and that is the part that decides most of it. It changes by legislature and the map linked above is the thing to check, not this page.

testing.reviewNote: Guidance here changes. Re-verify against DanceSafe, LAPPA, and manufacturer instructions before each release. Conflicts between sources are recorded rather than resolved.

framing.headline: Testing finds red flags. It never gives a green light.
canBullets: Tell you something you did not expect is present
Tell you the substance may not be what it was sold as
Give you information to decide how much to take, or whether to take it
cannotBullets: Tell you how strong it is
Tell you how pure it is
Tell you everything that is in it
Tell you whether fentanyl is in it
Read a bag the way a lab reads a reference sample
framing.ruleInRuleOut: A test can rule a substance IN. It cannot rule every other substance OUT.

sources.name: DanceSafe — Drug checking
Crew — Drug testing and checking

prevalence.headline: How often fentanyl actually turns up

rows.what: Sold as heroin or another opioid

rows.note: The bigger danger is that the amount varies wildly from pill to pill in the same batch.
Not zero, and worth testing — but not most.
One study of 53 samples found none.
Repeated investigations of alarming reports have not produced a single laboratory-confirmed case.

prevalence.coUse: You will also see that fentanyl appears alongside cocaine or meth in a huge share of overdose deaths. That is true, but it mostly reflects people using both — deliberately or at different times — not stimulants being secretly cut. The supply figures above and the death figures cannot both be explained by contamination. In one San Francisco study of overdoses, about 43% of people had not intended to take an opioid; the majority had.
prevalence.regional: These are national averages and they move. What is in the supply where you are can look nothing like the country as a whole, and it changes within months. Local drug-checking data beats any national number.
prevalence.bottomLine: The reason to test is not that everything is contaminated — it is that you cannot tell by looking. Testing is the only way to know what you are actually holding, and knowing changes what you can do about it.

sources.name: Russell et al. — fentanyl in stimulant samples, 25 states
Nguyen et al. — intent in non-fatal overdose, J Urban Health
UNC Street Drug Analysis Lab — The Year in Drugs
National Harm Reduction Coalition — fentanyl

strips.name: Fentanyl test strips
strips.detects: Fentanyl and many — not all — of its analogues

reading.invalid: No lines, or only a line on the end you dipped
reading.explain: This is backwards from a pregnancy test, and it is the single most misread part of drug checking. The strip works by competition: fentanyl in the sample blocks the test line from forming. The drug being present makes a line disappear.
reading.faintLine: A second line can be very faint and still count as negative. A faint line may also appear and then fade — wait the full three minutes before deciding.

procedure: Dissolve the drug in water. How much water depends on the drug and the brand of strip — see below.
Dip the wavy end (not the colored handle) into the solution — commonly about 15 seconds, but check your brand. Do not go past the dotted line.
Lay the strip flat on a dry surface.
Read at the time your instructions give — commonly 3 minutes. Do not read after 10 minutes; a strip left too long can change.

dilution.why: These strips were designed for urine. In water, some substances react with the antibody at high concentration and produce a FALSE POSITIVE. That is the only reason you are told to use more water for methamphetamine and MDMA — they cross-react. Cocaine and heroin do not, so they tolerate a stronger solution.

crossReact.threshold: no false positives found at tested concentrations

dilution.conflict: Published protocols disagree by as much as ten times — CDC, DanceSafe's website, DanceSafe's own printed brochure, and state health departments all give different water volumes. This is not sloppiness: the requirement genuinely differs by strip brand. BTNX 1.0 strips cross-react with meth and MDMA; DanceSafe/WHPM strips were found not to at the same concentration.
guidance: Follow the instructions that came with YOUR strips. Brands differ.
If you do not have them, use MORE water rather than less. Too little water causes false positives on stimulants; only extreme over-dilution risks a false negative.
If a stimulant tests positive, retest with about ten times more water before you act on it. In one street-sample study this corrected every false positive.

commonAmounts.amount: About 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of water per 10 mg
Crush the whole tablet into about 4 tablespoons. Undissolved binder is normal.
A small corner, soaked in 1 teaspoon for 10 minutes

commonAmounts.form: Residue in a cap, cooker or bag
commonAmounts.amount: About 1 mL of clean water onto the residue, after preparing a shot and before drawing it up

dilution.recovery: Testing does not destroy the drug — the water can be evaporated off afterwards.

limits.title: It does not mix evenly
limits.body: Fentanyl mixed into another drug is not distributed evenly. One side of a bag can hold none and the other enough to stop someone breathing. The strongest protection is to dissolve everything you intend to take, test that solution, and then take it. Second best: crush the whole batch to a fine powder and mix it thoroughly before taking a test portion.
limits.nuance: That study looked at batches where fentanyl was the main drug. Hot spots are a bigger risk when fentanyl is a contaminant in something else, and in pressed pills.

limits.title: It misses some analogues
limits.body: In a study of 251 synthetic opioids, 13 compounds were missed by both major brands. Each brand has its own blind spots — roughly 52 for DanceSafe/WHPM strips and 28 for BTNX, in different chemical directions.
limits.nuance: Carfentanil is genuinely disputed. One study found strips failed to detect it below very high concentrations; another found it detected across all lots; a third detected it in real street samples. Treat carfentanil detection as unreliable rather than assured.

limits.title: It does not detect nitazenes at all
limits.body: No fentanyl test strip detects nitazenes. All three nitazenes tested were missed by both brands. A negative fentanyl strip does not rule out a synthetic opioid.

limits.title: Sensitivity varies between batches
limits.body: Labels claim 10–20 ng/mL. Independent testing has found real thresholds as poor as 200 ng/mL. One study found 2017 lots hit 20 ng/mL, while 2021 lots of the same product only reached 200 ng/mL.

limits.title: The strip you buy today may be weaker than the one a study tested
limits.body: Comparing BTNX lots, 2017 strips detected fentanyl at 20 ng/mL while 2021 lots needed 200 ng/mL — a tenfold loss of sensitivity. Cross-reactivity moved the same way: false positives from diphenhydramine started at 100 mg/mL in the old lots and as low as 0.5 mg/mL in the new ones.
limits.nuance: So an accuracy number from a 2018 paper may not describe the strip in your hand in 2026. It is also why diluting properly matters more than which brand you buy.

sources.name: Halifax et al. 2024 — five BTNX lots

strips.accuracy: It was tested against 210 forensic samples. It missed 3.7% of the positives and called 9.6% positive when they were not. That is about 96% sensitivity and 90% specificity, down to 100 ng/mL.

sources.name: Green et al. 2020 — 210 forensic samples
DanceSafe FTS instructions (V19)
CDC — Fentanyl (overdose prevention)
Lockwood et al. — cross-reactivity
Assessment of 251 synthetic opioids
Ontario Drug Checking Community — FTS performance

strips.name: Xylazine test strips
strips.detects: Xylazine ("tranq"), a veterinary sedative found in the fentanyl supply — heavily in some regions, rarely in others

reading.invalid: No lines, or only a line on the dipped end
reading.explain: Same competitive format as fentanyl strips — one line means detected.

procedure: About 10 mg of drug — a match head, or a grain of rice — in 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of water. Mix well.
Wait 5 minutes — longer than a fentanyl strip.

limits.title: A negative result means much less here
limits.body: In a study of 333 fentanyl-positive street samples, xylazine strips caught only 49% of the samples that actually contained xylazine — 34 of 69. Most samples held less than 1% xylazine by weight, which is below what the strip can see. Roughly half of xylazine-positive samples read negative.

limits.title: False positives on older strips
limits.body: Version 1.0 strips cross-react with lidocaine, methamphetamine, ketamine, and diphenhydramine. The manufacturer says version 2.0 removed the lidocaine cross-reactivity, which matters because lidocaine is a standard cocaine cut. Independent evaluation of those claims is still pending — treat them as manufacturer statements, not verified fact.

limits.title: Naloxone does not reverse xylazine
limits.body: Xylazine is not an opioid. Naloxone will not reverse it — but almost all xylazine in the supply arrives alongside fentanyl, so you should still give naloxone. Watch breathing: if breathing improves, the naloxone worked, even if the person stays sedated.

sources.name: NYC Health — xylazine strip instructions
Community drug checking study, Los Angeles

strips.accuracy: A 2022 evaluation got 20 of 20 xylazine-positive samples right — but on strips that were not commercially available. Across seven brands you can actually buy, detection limits vary by more than double, with BTNX among the weaker ones. Levamisole, a common cocaine adulterant, causes false positives from 0.5 mg/mL.

strips.name: Benzodiazepine test strips
strips.detects: Benzodiazepines as a class — not which one

reading.invalid: No lines, or only a line on the dipped end

limits.title: Etizolam is the major gap
limits.body: Etizolam has a different ring structure that the antibody does not bind well, and it is one of the most common benzodiazepines found in the unregulated supply. Validation work reports high sensitivity only when etizolam samples are excluded from the count.

limits.title: Bromazolam IS detected
limits.body: Bromazolam — currently the most prevalent novel benzodiazepine in several unregulated supplies — is detected, because it shares the chemical core the antibody targets.

limits.title: Each new benzodiazepine is a coin flip
limits.body: Detection depends on chemical structure. A newly emerging benzodiazepine may or may not be caught, and there is no way to know until someone tests it specifically.

limits.title: A negative result can itself be informative
limits.body: If a pill sold as pharmaceutical alprazolam tests negative for benzodiazepines, that is a strong sign it is counterfeit.

sources.name: Benzodiazepine strip validation (2025)
Substance Drug Checking — benzodiazepine strips

strips.accuracy: On community drug-checking samples, benzodiazepine strips reached 98% sensitivity and 83% specificity — but only after etizolam-positive samples were removed from the analysis. A positive result was right about 56% of the time; a negative was right about 99% of the time.

strips.name: Nitazene test strips
strips.detects: Some nitazenes — a family of synthetic opioids that fentanyl strips miss entirely

reading.invalid: No lines, or only a line on the dipped end

limits.title: Nearly a third of real positives were missed
limits.body: In the only real-world evaluation, BTNX strips missed 29% of nitazene-positive street samples, and caffeine at 11–34% of a sample produced false positives. Readers also reported a very faint negative line on samples both with and without nitazenes, making results hard to call.
limits.nuance: Use them where nitazenes are circulating — a positive is real information. Do not treat a negative as clearance, and check the brand: performance between brands is not comparable.

sources.name: Ontario Drug Checking Community 2026 — 100 street samples

limits.title: Far less sensitive than fentanyl strips
limits.body: Cutoffs run 10 to 100 times higher than a fentanyl strip. One widely sold strip has a 2000 ng/mL cutoff against 10–20 ng/mL for fentanyl strips.

limits.title: Structural blind spots
limits.body: In lab evaluation, 24 of 33 nitazene analogues cross-reacted and 9 were undetectable. Analogues missing a particular chemical group are not detected at all.

limits.title: Still worth using if nitazenes are in your area
limits.body: Nitazene-involved overdose deaths in the US rose from 27 in 2020 to 409 in 2024. Naloxone does work on nitazenes, though multiple doses may be needed.

sources.name: Lab evaluation of nitazene strips

strips.accuracy: Lab results looked strong; real street samples did not. Against 100 samples checked by mass spectrometry, BTNX nitazene strips were 71% sensitive and 76% specific — a 29% false-negative rate. One other brand (Trimedic) was 11% sensitive, missing 89% of positives; that product does not work.

reagentIntro.cannotDetectFentanyl: Fentanyl works in amounts far too small for a reagent to see. Reagents react to the majority substance, not trace substances. Lab testing is what determines exactly what a substance is: FTIR for the bulk, GC-MS for traces like fentanyl.
masking: Not every drug reacts with every reagent
A darker color hides a lighter one
A very small amount of something may produce no visible change at all
reagentIntro.mixtures: Genuine mixtures blend like mixing two colors of paint. If you can see visually different crystals, separate them and test each one.

pureSampleNote.q: Does pure fentanyl react with a reagent?
pureSampleNote.a: In a forensic lab, yes — reference-grade fentanyl does produce a color change. It is irrelevant to anyone holding a bag. Drug checking in Los Angeles found consumer fentanyl averaged 10% fentanyl by weight, pills averaged 1.4%, and 42.5% of samples sold as fentanyl were under 5%. What you have is mostly filler, which is exactly the case reagents cannot read.
pureSampleNote.b: DanceSafe went through a public lab database. Oxycodone with fentanyl in it gave the same reagent colors as clean oxycodone. The pills that came back from overdose deaths looked correct.

reagents.name: Marquis
reagents.useFor: The broad first test. Start here.

reactions.color: Black, often purple or brown tinted
Gray to black — but DELAYED 15–30 seconds, often smoking
reactions.note: The timing, not the final color, is what separates DXM from MDMA

reactions.color: Disputed — no reaction, or light pink to deep peach
reactions.note: Bright orange or red here may mean an amphetamine is present instead

caveats: Cocaine is disputed. Older forensic sources say no reaction; DanceSafe updated in 2023 to expect anything from no reaction to a deep peach or light pink. Bright orange or red on cocaine may mean an amphetamine is present.

reagents.name: Mecke
reagents.base: Selenous acid in concentrated sulfuric acid
caveats: DanceSafe marks Mecke as unvalidated for MDMA/MDA even though it is widely sold as an MDMA reagent.

reagents.name: Simon's
reagents.base: Two-part: sodium nitroprusside with acetaldehyde, then sodium carbonate. Aqueous and alkaline, not an acid.
reagents.useFor: The only common reagent that separates MDMA from MDA, and methamphetamine from amphetamine. Always a second test, never a first.
caveats: The textbook rule that MDA gives no reaction is no longer reliable. Since about 2021 MDA-like substances may produce a muddy gray-green. Both outcomes are now expected, and older charts still teach the old rule.
Listed as inconsistent for 2C-B — do not use it to characterize 2C-x compounds.

reagents.name: Mandelin
reagents.base: Ammonium metavanadate in concentrated sulfuric acid
caveats: Sources disagree on whether to carry it at all. One vendor discontinued it for short shelf life and false positives; another still recommends it for PMA/PMMA screening. DanceSafe marks it unvalidated for MDMA/MDA.
It starts light orange and turns cloudy yellow after 3–4 weeks. That is normal — shake before use.

reagents.name: Froehde
reagents.base: Molybdic acid in hot concentrated sulfuric acid
reagents.useFor: Confirmatory third data point; strong on opioids and MDMA
caveats: Sources conflict on amphetamines: one sequences Froehde as a step for meth/amphetamine, another states no color change. Do not rely on a specific Froehde-amphetamine color.

reagents.name: Liebermann
reagents.base: Potassium or sodium nitrite in concentrated sulfuric acid
reagents.useFor: Secondary reagent for cocaine and ketamine; responds to levamisole

reactions.color: Light yellow to orange — a range is accepted
Very pale yellow, sometimes nearly invisible

caveats: Liebermann alone cannot separate cocaine from a cathinone — both land in the yellow range.

reagents.name: Ehrlich's
reagents.base: p-DMAB in ethanol with concentrated hydrochloric acid
reagents.useFor: The indole reagent, and the single most important LSD test. Use only for LSD and DMT.

reactions.color: Positive, via tryptophan — a genuine false-positive trap

caveats: A negative result on blotter does not mean nothing is there. It fits an NBOMe just as well. That is the thing most often sold as LSD, and it is far more dangerous.
Slow reagent — can take up to 5 minutes, and stays readable for up to an hour.
Ehrlich's does turn purple for psilocybin. It also turns purple for indoles in general, including supermarket mushrooms and death cap. So it cannot tell you a species.

reagents.name: Morris
reagents.useFor: The ketamine and cocaine reagent — the only common reagent giving a strong distinctive ketamine result

reactions.note: Know this color — too small a sample lets the green tint muddy a real result

caveats: Not very sensitive: detection limits are around 1.25 mg.
A "not ketamine" result does not identify what it actually is. Several newer dissociatives are uncharacterized.

procedure.title: Use a pinhead of sample
procedure.body: Finely crushed. Blotter: a tiny corner. Liquids: one drop. Morris: double. For low-dose pressed pills use MORE — a 150 mg pill may hold only 10 mg of active drug.

procedure.title: Never test the whole pill, and never in the bag
procedure.body: Use a white, clean, dry, non-porous surface — ceramic or hard plastic. These reagents are concentrated acids and will destroy a plastic bag. Testing the whole pill destroys the dose and gives an unreadable smear. Pill and blotter dyes distort colors: orange pills throw orange specks, blue pills read muddy brown, and blotter dye is easily mistaken for a purple Ehrlich's positive.

procedure.title: One drop, and never touch the sample with the bottle
procedure.body: Touching the tip to the sample contaminates the entire bottle. Hold the cap upside down while you work — setting it down, or on the wrong bottle, is a common mistake. For two-part reagents, both drops go on the SAME sample.

procedure.title: Watch from the moment the drop lands
procedure.body: Intermediate colors carry information — that is how Marquis separates MDMA from DXM. Read within roughly the first minute and disregard later drift from air and moisture. Sources give anywhere from 40 seconds to 3 minutes, so there is no single correct number. Ehrlich's, Hofmann, and Morris are the slow exceptions at about 5 minutes.

procedure.title: Use several reagents, with a fresh sample each time
procedure.body: Never drop a second reagent onto an already-tested spot. Re-cap before opening the next bottle. One reagent narrows it down; several together tell you much more, because each one rules out something different.

procedure.title: Run a blank next to it
procedure.body: Put a drop of the reagent alone beside your test spot. Reagents are tinted and darken with age, so a blank tells you what "no reaction" looks like today. Use neutral daylight. If unsure, retest with a larger sample.

procedure.title: Clean up
procedure.body: Neutralize with baking soda, wash with soap and water, and dry before the next test.

safety.ppe: Wear gloves and eye protection. Marquis, Mecke, Mandelin, Froehde, Liebermann and Hofmann are concentrated sulfuric acid; Ehrlich's is hydrochloric acid in ethanol. They damage skin and eyes. Work in a ventilated area — DXM on Marquis often smokes.
firstAid: Eyes: flood with water for at least 10 minutes, holding the eye open.
Swallowed: rinse the mouth, do NOT induce vomiting, drink water, get medical help immediately.
safety.storage: Keep upright, lid secured, away from heat and light. Refrigerated they last 1–2 years; at room temperature that roughly halves. Let them warm up before opening, since condensation and cold change how they react.
safety.expiry: Marquis and Mecke darken as they age. A reagent is expired when it is too dark to read a reaction clearly. Dark green or black means contamination — discard it.
safety.validate: Test a drop on sugar. If you cannot see a clear reaction, the reagent may no longer be accurate.
safety.disposal: Neutralize the spent drop with baking soda and rinse the surface with plenty of water. Take unused or expired reagent to a household hazardous waste facility. Never pour concentrated acid neat down a drain, and never mix reagents together.

legal.headline: Test strips are legal in most, but not all, states
legal.body: The same carve-out covers xylazine strips in 36 states plus DC. Ohio and Florida joined after the earlier count. Reagent kits are covered in fewer states still. So a strip that is legal for one drug may not be legal for another.
legal.stale: Lists circulating online are out of date. Idaho changed in July 2024 and Indiana in 2025, so the commonly repeated five-state list is wrong. As of July 2026 the three remaining states where possessing drug-checking equipment may still be criminal are Iowa, North Dakota and Texas.
legal.advice: Check your own state's current law. Nothing here is legal advice.

labs.intro: Only a laboratory can confirm what is actually in a sample. Most of these take samples through a harm reduction program rather than from individuals — check each one before you post anything.
labs.note: DrugsData.org paused accepting new samples in April 2024 and does not expect to resume before 2027. Its historical archive is still worth searching, but do not mail samples there.

how.title: What a lab does that a strip cannot
how.intro: A strip answers one yes/no question about one substance. These identify everything in a sample, and some of them say how much.

methods.name: FTIR — infrared spectroscopy
methods.what: Shines infrared light through the sample and reads which wavelengths it absorbs. Every compound has a distinct absorption pattern, so the machine matches that pattern against a library.
methods.good: Seconds to run, no sample destroyed, and it is what most in-person drug checking services actually use — you can often watch it happen and ask questions.
methods.limits: It reads the BULK of a sample. Anything under roughly 5% by weight can be invisible to it, which means it routinely misses fentanyl at street concentrations. That is why services run FTIR and a fentanyl strip together, not one instead of the other.

methods.name: GC-MS — gas chromatography–mass spectrometry
methods.what: Separates a mixture into its individual components, then weighs each one's molecular fragments to identify it. The chromatography does the separating; the mass spectrometry does the identifying.
methods.good: The reference standard. It finds trace components an FTIR cannot see, including fentanyl analogues and adulterants present in tiny amounts, and it names them specifically rather than by family.
methods.limits: Needs a laboratory, trained staff, and days rather than seconds. This is what mail-in programs use, and the wait is the trade-off for the detail.

methods.name: LC-MS and NMR
methods.what: Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry handles compounds that GC cannot vaporize. NMR reads how atomic nuclei behave in a magnetic field and can determine structure and quantity.
methods.good: Together these give quantitative answers — not just what is present, but how much. That is the only way to know a percentage rather than a yes.
methods.limits: The most expensive and least available. Only a handful of programs offer it.

how.bottom: Nothing here is instant, and none of it tells you about the batch you did not send. What a lab result changes is what you know about your supply in general — and, through published results, what everyone else in your area knows too.

companion: A smaller amount first, with time before any more, is what tells you about a batch before it tells you the hard way. It matters most with something new, or after any time away — tolerance drops faster than people expect.

Using alone is what turns most overdoses into accidents — not the dose, the fact that nobody was there to notice. If there is no one around, Never Use Alone answers 24/7 at 1-800-484-3731 and sends help if you stop responding.
Carry naloxone, and make sure whoever is with you knows where it is.
Fentanyl and nitazenes are opioids — naloxone works on both. It may take more than one dose.

storage.headline: Storing your supplies
storage.intro: Every one of these degrades, and a degraded test does not announce itself — it just gives you a wrong answer in the same confident colors.

items.what: Reagents
items.how: Fridge if you can, dark and cool if you cannot. Keep them in the box they came in.
items.why: Light and heat break them down. Reagents darken with age — a Marquis that has gone brown on its own will read as a reaction that never happened. This is why running a blank drop beside your test matters: it shows you what the bottle looks like today.
items.life: Roughly a year refrigerated, much less if warm. Replace them if the color has drifted.

items.what: Test strips
items.how: Room temperature, sealed in their pouch until the moment you use one. Not the glovebox, not the bathroom.
items.why: Humidity is the enemy — the pouch is sealed for a reason, and a strip that has taken on moisture can fail in either direction. Heat cycling in a car does the same.
items.life: Check the printed expiry. An expired strip is not a maybe.

items.what: Naloxone
items.how: Room temperature, out of direct light, somewhere you can reach it in the dark and someone else can find it.
items.why: It tolerates ordinary conditions well but not extremes. A car in summer or a freezing porch is genuinely too much. Nasal spray works fine after freezing IF it has fully thawed — but if you only have one dose, do not rely on that.
items.life: Expiry dates are conservative. Expired naloxone loses potency over time but is far better than none — if it is what you have, use it and call 911.

items.what: Anything shared or hidden
items.how: Somewhere another person can find it without you telling them where.
items.why: Naloxone in a locked box in your room helps nobody if you are the one who is not breathing. Whoever is around needs to know it exists and be able to reach it.

compare.headline: Which test tells you what
compare.intro: No single tool answers every question, and the differences between them are not small. This is the short version; each tool has its own section below with the detail and the sources.
compare.note: Every one of these is better at saying yes than at saying no. They also do better in a lab than on real street samples. The numbers here are the street ones.

rows.finds: Fentanyl and many of its analogues
rows.misses: Nitazenes entirely. Some analogues. Uneven mixing in a bag.
rows.negative: Fairly strong — about 96% sensitivity against 210 forensic samples. But sensitivity varies tenfold between manufacturing lots, so dilute properly.

rows.misses: Medetomidine, which is now replacing xylazine in some places and does not cross-react.
rows.negative: Weak. A negative rules out xylazine, not sedation — medetomidine does not cross-react. Levamisole causes false positives.

rows.finds: Benzodiazepines as a class — never which one
rows.misses: Etizolam, the major gap. Each newly appearing benzo is a coin flip.
rows.negative: Moderate. 98% sensitive only once etizolam samples are excluded; a positive is right about 56% of the time.

rows.finds: Some nitazenes — the family fentanyl strips miss
rows.misses: Structural blind spots; far less sensitive than fentanyl strips.
rows.negative: Weak — 29% of real positives were missed in the only street-sample study, and one brand missed 89%. A positive means something; a negative does not.

rows.finds: What the BULK of a sample mostly is
rows.misses: Anything present in small amounts — including fentanyl at street concentrations. Colors can mask each other in a mixture.
rows.negative: Different question entirely. Reagents identify the main substance; they do not screen for contaminants.

rows.misses: Nothing technical — the limit is time and access.
rows.negative: Strongest available. The trade-off is days of turnaround and, for most people, going through a local program.

buying.headline: Buying it over the counter
buying.intro: The same shelf carries a product that looks almost the same and answers a completely different question. So it is worth knowing exactly what to pick up.

trap.title: Most “fentanyl test strips” sold in stores test a person, not a drug
trap.body: A urine drug screen tells you whether someone has already taken something. It cannot tell you what is in a bag. Both are strips in a pouch, both are immunoassays, and they sit in the same aisle under nearly the same words.
trap.tell: How to tell them apart: a substance-checking kit comes with a micro-scoop and a small measuring cup, because you dissolve a sample in water. A urine screen mentions urine, a dip card or cassette, a panel count, or “CLIA waived”. If it costs more and includes a mail-in lab envelope, it is a urine screen.
trap.examples: Verified in August 2026: Walmart’s entire “fentanyl strips” category — all 23 results — was urine screens. CVS sells both, with the urine kit at roughly twice the price of the real thing, and its own listing text mixed up which drug it tests for.

items.price: About $35 for a two-dose Narcan carton at CVS

items.note: Programs stock up through Grassroots Harm Reduction. It is a buyers' club, open to any group that gives supplies away free. If you run a program, or want to start one, that is where the supply comes from.

legal.title: Whether you can buy them depends on your state
legal.body: Drug-checking equipment is fully legal to sell, give away and possess in 20 states. Thirteen more allow it only for specific drugs — usually fentanyl strips. In Iowa, North Dakota and Texas, possessing it arguably remains a crime. Puerto Rico's status is unknown rather than clear — the July 2026 review covers four of five territories without naming which ones. Massachusetts and Michigan allow possession and free distribution but not sale.
legal.note: These laws are actively changing. The counts above are from a July 2026 review; anything you read elsewhere without a date on it is probably older. Availability varies by store and by state and cannot be verified nationally — if a chain near you does not carry it, a local harm reduction program can.

brands.headline: Which strip do you have?
brands.intro: Two fentanyl strips are in wide use. One wants five times more water than the other. They are read two minutes apart. And they do not find the same things.

notInterchangeable.body: That is not a reason to distrust the one you have. It is the reason a negative result is weaker than a positive one. It is also why programs hand out both when they can.

items.name: Grassroots Harm Reduction
items.maker: Also the WHPM strip, made in Irwindale, California and built for drug checking rather than urine screening. Cut-off 10 ng/mL.
items.sample: 50 mg of drug into one teaspoon of water — 10 mg per mL, the same concentration as the other WHPM strips.
items.water: 5 mL — one teaspoon — for every 50 mg.
items.residue: Testing residue instead? That is what is left in a cap, a cooker, or the corner of a bag. Add 2 mL of clean water, about half a teaspoon, and mix well.
items.dip: Dip for 15 seconds, holding the colored end. Grassroots does not restate the timings on its product page; these are the WHPM strip's published procedure.
items.dipLimit: Do not dip above the dotted section.
items.negative: TWO red lines — any second line, however faint, is negative
items.invalid: No lines, or only the bottom line. Redo it with a new strip.
items.blindSpot: A WHPM strip, so it shares WHPM's blind spot: bulky carbonyl modifications. What it does not do is false-positive on meth, MDMA, lidocaine or levamisole at 10 mg/mL, which laboratory testing checked for specifically.

items.name: BTNX Rapid Response
items.sample: 10 mg of drug — about a match head or a grain of rice — crushed and mixed.
items.water: 5 mL of water for every 10 mg — one teaspoon. If you cook a shot, that is a full cooker.
items.dip: Dip for 15 seconds, holding the solid end.
items.dipLimit: Do not dip past the wavy red lines.
items.negative: TWO red lines — if two appear, however faint, it is negative
items.invalid: A line only on the left, or no lines at all. Redo it with a new strip.
items.onlyFor: Only use these on fentanyl. They can read positive on cocaine and other drugs when no xylazine is there.

brands.gap: Wondfo, DetectaChem, Lochness Medical and MD-Bio are not here yet. Neither are benzodiazepine or nitazene strips. We only print a number once we have read it off the sheet it came from.
brands.notListed: Not listed? Most strips sold for harm reduction in the US are made by one of two companies — BTNX or WHPM — whatever name is on the front. DanceSafe, Bunk Police and Grassroots all sell the same WHPM strip. Look for the maker on the packet, the box or the insert and use that row. If it names neither, your insert is the authority.
brands.lotsTitle: Read the instructions that came with your strips
brands.lots: Strips are not interchangeable, and a brand can change between lots. Dip time, how long a result stays valid and how much water to use have all differed between batches from the same maker. The row above is that product's published procedure; the paper in your packet is that packet's.
